We place that nourishment of his within our reach, he who is more clearly visible by night than by day, more visible by day than to one whose life is spent;
from him comes a life that is firm to grasp, like a secure shelter for a son. May the ageless fires grant us shared and unshared protection; the ageless fires grant it.
For he, roaring loudly like the host of Maruts, is the one who bestows gifts upon the fertile fields and bestows gifts upon the dry lands;
he takes up the offerings, the taker, the banner of sacrifice, worthy of honor.
And indeed, when he is exhilarated and full of joy, all men delight in his path, as they do in the path for a glorious display.
When the *kīstas* who look toward heaven, the *Bhṛgus*, calling him with reverence, have invoked him—the *Bhṛgus* churning [the fire]—then Agni rules over riches, he who is their pure sustainer.
May the wise one win the beloved secret coverings; may the wise one win them.

We invoke you, the lord of all people, the common husband of them all, for our enjoyment; we invoke the one borne by true hymns, for our enjoyment. He is the guest of human beings, like a father, through whose presence [we thrive].
And may all these immortals come to our offerings among the gods; may they come to our strengthening food.

O Agni, you are born as the most victorious by your power, the most impetuous for the sake of the gods, like wealth for the sake of the gods. For your intoxication is most impetuous, and your wisdom is most splendid.
Therefore, O ageless one, they attend upon you, like obedient servants, O ageless one.

Let your hymn of praise go forth to the great Agni, who by his might overcomes the mighty, who awakens at dawn, and who bestows cattle—let it go forth to Agni. When the one possessing oblations calls out to him in all lands, he, like a singer, awakens before the flames; he is the ancient Hotṛ-priest among the flames.

May he, appearing most near to us, O Agni, bring hither with the gods and with gracious wisdom—yea, with gracious wisdom—great wealth. O mightiest one, grant us greatness that we may behold and enjoy this;
O Maghavan, churn out great heroic power for those who praise you, like a fierce one by his own strength.
This Agni was born for the support of man, the most excellent invoker according to the vow of the *uśij*, according to his own vow;
he who hears all, like wealth for one seeking friendship, for one seeking renown.
The undeceivable invoker has sat down in the place of *iḷā*, encircled in the place of *iḷā*.
I send him forth, the accomplisher of sacrifice, along the path of *ṛta* with reverence and an oblation, at the assembly of the gods with an oblation. May he,
bringing us strength through this form of his, never grow old—
he whom Mātariśvan brought from afar for Manu, the god of light from afar.
By his even path he traverses the earthly realm at once; the bull, bellowing repeatedly, pours forth his seed as he bellows.
Beholding with a hundred eyes, the god prevails within the woods. Agni establishes his seat upon the lower ridges and upon the highest ridges.

He, the wise one, the domestic priest, in every house, Agni takes heed of the sacrifice and the ritual; by his mental power he takes heed of the sacrifice. By his mental power the Ordainer is implored; he has observed all created beings.
From whence the guest adorned with clarity was born, from whence the bearer and the Ordainer was born.
When they mingle with his powers through wisdom, like the Maruts with the roar of Agni, he is for the impetuous one as food is for the hungry;
for he indeed promotes the gift of riches by his greatness. May he protect us from misfortune and from assault, from the curse and from evil assault.

All-pervading, far-reaching, and wealthy, he has placed the sacrificial ladle in his right hand; like one who crosses over, he does not loosen his hold; out of desire for glory, he does not loosen it.
For every supplicant, you have brought the oblation among the gods.
To every doer of good, Agni grants a boon; he throws open the doors.

He has been established as the most peaceful one in the human community; Agni is like a noble lord of the people at the sacrifices, the beloved lord of the people at the sacrifices. He rules over the oblations of men prepared with *iḷā* offerings. May he protect us from the malice of Varuṇa, from the malice of the great god.
They praise Agni as the Hotṛ-priest, the bestower of wealth; they have established him as the beloved, most wise steward; they have established him as the carrier of oblations.
The gods, seeking riches, have established with songs the one who sustains all life, the all-knowing, the worshipful sage, the Hotṛ—him who is delightful for their protection, seeking riches.
O Indra, that chariot which you, O impetuous one, lead forward from behind for the winning of the prize—O blameless one, you lead it on;
you instantly make it victorious for our assistance, according to your will. O blameless and impetuous one, accept this speech of ours, as [you have accepted] the speech of the wise.
Hear us, O Indra, you who are to be honored by men in every battle when the call to arms is raised; you are with the men for the sake of victory.

You who, with heroes, win the light of heaven, and with the inspired singers, overcome for the prize—him, the powerful one, the masters entreat like a swift steed, like a vigorous horse that brings nourishment.

For as a wondrous worker, you cause the bull-like skin to swell; you ward off every stingy mortal, O hero, you exclude the mortal. Indra, I declare this to you, to Heaven, and to Rudra who is self-glorious;
I proclaim it to Mitra and Varuṇa far and wide, for their great mercy far and wide.
We desire Indra for our protection—the friend who possesses all life, the ally who overcomes in battles, the ally who overcomes in battles. May our sacred prayer protect us in every conflict;
for no enemy can strike you down, you who strike down every enemy, you who strike him down.
Bend down the overweening pride of anyone with your most sharpened kindling-sticks, with your aids—O fierce one, with your fierce aids!
Lead us as you did of old; O Hero, you consider us sinless.
As a bearer, carry us across all [difficulties] of the Pūru; as a bearer, bring us hither by your mouth.

I would proclaim this to the future Soma-drop, who, like one to be invoked, possesses the power of the sacrifice; he, the slayer of demons, stirs the prayer, he stirs the prayer. May he himself drive away from us the ill-wisher with his weapons, the evil-minded one.
May the one who utters evil flow away downward, may he flow away like a tiny speck of dust.
May we win that through thoughtful invocation; may we win wealth, O Lord of Wealth, with excellent heroic power—wealth that is delightful and full of heroic power.
May we approach the ill-minded one with auspicious thoughts and with nourishment. With true invocations of glory, let us worship Indra, the holy one, with invocations of glory.

Forward and ever forward for us come your aids, O Indra, with your own glories; you are the one who excludes the ill-minded and shatters the ill-minded. May that [hostile power] which has approached us with its devouring jaws perish of itself.
Let it be struck down; let it not carry us away, nor shall the hurled flame carry us off.

O Indra, come to us with abundant wealth by a path free from danger; go before us on a path devoid of demons. Be with us in the distance, be with us at home. Protect us from afar and from near at hand with your aids; protect us always with your aids.
O Indra, may you [grant] us wealth that overcomes; may your greatness accompany even the fierce one for our great protection, as one seeks a friend for protection.
O strongest one, O protector, O immortal, be the helper of whatever chariot there may be.
O wielder of the stone, harm no one other than us; O wielder of the stone, harm even him who intends to harm us.
Protect us from harm, O Indra, you who are well-praised; as a god, you are forever the warder-off of the ill-minded, the warder-off of the malicious.
You are the slayer of the evil *rakṣas* and the protector of a sage such as I.
For thus did the progenitor beget you, O Vasu; he begot you, O Vasu, as the slayer of *rakṣases*.

O Indra, come to us from afar, as a lord of the virtuous comes toward the assemblies, as a king comes to his home, O lord of the virtuous. We invoke you while offering oblations at the pressed juice, like sons invoking a father for the winning of booty— invoking the most bountiful one for the winning of booty.

Drink the Soma pressed by the stones, O Indra, poured from the vessel like a bull who has found water, like a bull parched with thirst. For your exhilaration, for your beloved state, for your most powerful nourishment— let the bay steeds bring you hither as they bring the sun, as all the days bring the sun.
He found the treasure hidden in the cave of heaven, like the embryo of a bird enveloped within the rock, within the infinite rock.
Like one desiring to win a stall of cattle, Indra, the wielder of the thunderbolt, the best of the Aṅgirases, threw open the doors;
Indra threw open the doors of the enclosed food, the enclosed refreshments.
Firmly grasping the thunderbolt in his two hands, Indra whetted it like a sharp blade for hurling; he whetted it for the slaying of Ahi.
Enveloped in might, in powers, and in majesty, O Indra, you hew down the forest trees like a carpenter with an axe; you hew them down like an axe.
O Indra, you have released the rivers to flow at will toward the ocean, like chariots, like prize-seeking chariots. From here they have harnessed their aids for a common, inexhaustible purpose—
like milch-cows yielding all things for mankind, yielding all things for the people.
Seeking wealth, these Āyus have fashioned this speech for you, as a skillful craftsman fashions a chariot; they have fashioned you for favor.
O Sage, adorning you like a noble steed for the sake of booty in battles, we have made you like a courser for power, for the winning of riches—for the winning of all riches.

O Indra, O dancer, you shattered ninety forts for Pūru Divodāsa, the great donor, for the sake of the donor, O dancer; with your thunderbolt, O fierce one, you brought down Śambara from the mountain for Atithigva.
Distributing vast treasures by your might, you distributed all treasures by your might.

Indra, who possesses a hundredfold aid, protected the Aryan sacrificer in battles, in all contests for light, in the struggles for booty. Governing for Manu, he subdued the lawless; he made the black skin subject to him.
Like fire, he burns every thirsty foe; he utterly consumes the malicious one.
The Sun, having been born with power, forced open the wheel; at the onset of the day, the ruddy one steals away the voice; as the sovereign lord, he steals it away.
When Uśanas came from afar for help, O Sage, he won all blessings like Manu, winning them all like the days.
O you of heroic deeds, destroyer of forts, protect us with your powerful guardians through our new hymns;
O Indra, being praised by the Divodāsas, may you increase like the sky grows by the days.
For to Indra has Dyaus, the Asura, bowed down; to Indra has the great Earth bowed with her vast expanses, in the winning of glory, with her vast expanses.
All the gods, acting in harmony, have placed Indra at their head.
For Indra let all the libations of men be offered—let them be the gifts of men.
For at all the libations, those who long for the bull urge you on—the seekers of light, each separately, the seekers of the sun, each separately.
We set you, like a ship that carries us across, at the pole of our strength;
the Āyus distinguish Indra with sacrifices, the Āyus with hymns of praise.
Couples seeking your aid have spread themselves out for you, O Indra, as they strive to win the stall of cattle, they who release you, they who overcome you.
When you bring together two men seeking cattle or seeking the light of heaven,
you roar aloud, O Indra, manifesting the bull-like thunderbolt that is your constant companion.
The Pūrus knew of this heroic power of yours, O Indra, when you overthrew the autumnal fortresses—you, the conqueror, overthrew them.
You chastised that mortal who does not sacrifice, O Indra, Lord of Might;
you seized the great earth and these waters while rejoicing—these very waters.
Then indeed they celebrated this heroic deed of yours in the exhilarations, O Bull, when you, the one who desires [the sacrifice], protected them; when you protected those who sought your friendship.
You performed a great deed for them so that they might prevail in battles.
Desiring glory, they won river after river; desiring glory, they won.
And may he be pleased with us at this dawn; indeed, take note of our hymn and our oblations through our invocations, in the winning of the light through our invocations.
O Indra, wielder of the thunderbolt, when you, the bull, intend to slay the adversaries, listen to this prayer of mine, the most recent of the worshipper, listen to the prayer of the most recent one.

O Indra, growing strong and well-disposed toward us, O hero of many births, slay with your thunderbolt that mortal who acts as an enemy, that mortal who seeks to harm us. Listen, you who are most renowned;
let ill-will be driven away from our path like a mishap, let all ill-will be dispelled.
O Maghavan, with you as our protector, O Indra, may we overcome those who attack us and conquer those who seek to harm us, as we won wealth in the ancient days.
On this most immediate day, speak now in favor of the one who presses the soma;
at this sacrifice, may we, seeking booty, distribute the prize won in battle—the prize won in battle.
In the winning of light, bring [the prize] in the recitation of the *āprī*-hymn, for the one who awakens at dawn, in his own adornment; for the one who acts, in his own adornment.
Indra slew [the foe], as is well known—he who is to be praised head by head.
May your gifts be directed toward us; may the gifts of the auspicious one be auspicious.
That ancient offering of thine has shone forth as of old, at that sacrifice where they made the dwelling place their choice; thou art the chooser, the dwelling place of the Eternal Law (*ṛta*).
Proclaim that even now in two ways; they behold within with their rays.
Indeed, Indra is known as the seeker of cattle, the seeker of cattle for those who dwell in kinship.
Now indeed, as in the past, this deed of yours is to be proclaimed—that you opened up the stall for the Aṅgirases, O Indra, opening the stall out of your favor.
Toward them, and in the same direction, may you conquer and fight for us;
subject to those who press the Soma every lawless man, even the one who is wrathful and lawless.

When the Hero has united the people with his powers of will, they gaze upon him; when the prize is set, those seeking glory strive for victory, those seeking glory press forward. To him they sing for long life accompanied by progeny, even in the face of oppression, with their might.
The prayers desire to win him as their own home; the prayers go forth toward the Gods.
O Indra and Parvata, you who fight from the front, strike down each and every one who would attack us; strike him down with the thunderbolt, strike him down!
May it reach the one who stays afar, even the thicket he seeks to enter.
O Hero, may you, the destroyer, crush our enemies on all sides; may you crush them everywhere.
I purify both worlds with cosmic order; I burn up the great, Indra-less deceivers.
Where the enemies were struck down after being hemmed in, they lay scattered all around at Vailasthāna.
O wielder of the stone, having utterly crushed the heads of the sorceresses, cut them off with your wide-spreading foot, with your great wide-spreading foot.
O Maghavan, strike down this host of sorceresses;
[strike them] at Vailasthānaka, at Armaka, at Mahāvailastha, and at Armaka.
Of those fifty-three [stems] which you stripped away with your claws—that indeed provokes your thought; that truly provokes your thought.
O Indra, crush the Piśāca with his tawny-tipped, glowing weapon;
strike down every demon.

O great Indra, rend asunder [the obstacles]; hear us! For heaven has glowed with fear, like the earth, O wielder of the stone, from fear; like the sun’s heat, O wielder of the stone, from fear. For you, the most powerful one, advance with your powerful weapons and your fierce [blows].
You are the slayer of those who do not protect men, O unassailable hero, with your thrice-seven heroic warriors, O hero, with your heroic warriors.
For the one who presses the juice wins a dwelling of abundance; for the one who presses the juice indeed overcomes his enemies—the enemies of the gods, the enemies he overcomes.
The one who presses the juice, an unimpeded seeker of strength, desires to win thousands. To the one who presses the juice, Indra gives enduring wealth; he gives enduring wealth.
May the swift, rushing [horses] bring you here to the offerings, O Vāyu, for the first draught of Soma, for the first draught!
May our true speech stand upright before your mind, knowing [you].
Come with your chariot drawn by teams of horses to give, O Vāyu, to give the gift of the sacrifice!
May the gladdening drops, O Vāyu, made by us, well-prepared and directed toward heaven, delight you—made with milk, directed toward heaven.

When the aids, being prepared, attend to the skillful one for the sake of attainment, may the prayers, the teams of horses moving in unison, and the hymns speak to him for the granting of gifts; yea, the hymns speak to him.
Vāyu yokes the two ruddy steeds; Vāyu yokes the two tawny ones; Vāyu yokes the two swift ones to the chariot to draw at the pole, the best at drawing at the pole.
Awaken Purandhi, as a lover awakens a sleeping woman.
Make the two worlds visible; clothe the dawns for glory, clothe the dawns for glory.
For you, the bright dawns in the distance spread out their auspicious garments within your wondrous rays—bright garments within your new rays.
For you, the cow who milks at will yields all treasures.
From your flanks you brought forth the Maruts, from the flanks of heaven.
For you, the bright, pure, and swift drops, fierce in their exhilaration, have sped toward the world; they have sped toward the world.
The weary hunter, seeking his prey, prays to you for fortune in the chase.
You protect [us] from every being by your law; you protect us from the divine power by your law.

O Vāyu, you who are without predecessor, you deserve the first draught of these pressed Soma juices; you deserve the draught. And for the tribes that have offered worship and turned toward you—with all those cows they milk out the milk-mixture for you; they milk out the clarified butter and the milk-mixture.
The sacrificial grass is strewn; come to us for the feast with a thousand teams, O Lord of Teams, with hundreds of teams, O Lord of Teams!
For the gods have directed themselves toward you, the god, for the first draught.
The sweet-pressed juices have stood forth for you; they have stood forth for exhilaration, for the sake of your will.
For you this Soma, purified by the stones and clothed in desirable riches, flows around the vat; clothed in brilliance, it flows.
This portion of yours among mortals—Soma—is offered among the gods.
O Vāyu, bring your teams; come seeking us; enjoying [the offering], come seeking us.
Come to our sacrifice with your teams of horses, by the hundreds and by the thousands, for the feast—to Vāyu, for the feast upon the oblations!
This is your seasonal portion, accompanied by the rays along with the sun.
Brought by the *adhvaryu* priests, the bright drops have been offered; O Vāyu, the bright drops have been offered.
May your chariot, drawn by teams of horses, bring you both for our protection, toward the well-prepared offerings for your enjoyment, O Vāyu, toward the oblations for your enjoyment.
Drink of the sweet juice; for the first draught is ordained for you both.
O Vāyu, come with radiant bounty; and Indra, come with bounty.
May our prayers turn you both toward the sacrifices; they have cleansed this vigorous drop like a swift, prize-winning steed.
Drink of these, O you who are well-disposed toward us; come hither to us with your speed!
Indra and Vāyu, you two are the givers of strength; drink of the juices pressed by the stones for your exhilaration.
These Soma juices, pressed here in the waters for you both, have been offered by the Adhvaryu priests; O Vāyu, the bright juices have been offered.
These swift ones have been poured forth for you both across the filter;
seeking you, the Soma drops have passed through the sheep’s wool, past the sheep’s wool.
O Vāyu, pass by all those who sleep; go to that place where the pressing-stone speaks—go to the house, and may Indra also go there.
Generosity has become visible; the clarified butter flows. Come to the sacrifice with a full team of horses, and may Indra also come to the sacrifice.
Here, O Vāyu, you two carry that offering of honey; the swift steeds attend upon that *aśvattha* tree—may they be swift for us.
Together the cows bring forth their milk, the barley ripens; your milch-cows do not fail, O Vāyu, your milch-cows do not fail.
O Vāyu, these which are yours, possessing the strength of arms— these bulls fly within the rivers, swelling greatly, these bulls; even those that are not swift on the desert plain,
though they are agile and dwell not in the mountains, like the rays of the sun, they are difficult to restrain, difficult to restrain by the hands.
Bring forth the highest, great homage—the oblation and the prayer—to the two attentive ones who are gracious, the most sweet [offering] to those who are gracious.
Those two sovereign kings, whose food is clarified butter, are praised at every sacrifice. Thus, their dominion is not to be assailed from any quarter; their divinity is never to be assailed.
A wider path has been seen for the broad world; the way of *ṛta* has been aligned with its rays—the eye of Bhaga with its rays.
The celestial dwelling of Mitra, Aryaman, and Varuṇa is now revealed.
Thus they two bestow great, praiseworthy vigor—great, hymn-worthy vigor.
They attend to Aditi, who is luminous, upholding the earth, and full of light, day after day, they who are ever-watchful day by day.
The two Ādityas have attained a radiant dominion; they are the lords of bounty.
Of these two, Mitra and Varuṇa are the stirrers of the people, and Aryaman is the stirrer of the people.
May this Soma, becoming most propitious for Mitra and Varuṇa, be a sharer in the drinking-vessels; may the god be a sharer among the gods.
May all the gods today take pleasure in it with one accord. O Kings, you who uphold the cosmic order, grant us that which we implore, even that for which we pray.

The man who serves Mitra and Varuṇa with worship, him they protect from distress—the unassailable mortal who offers oblations—from distress. Aryaman guards him who acts uprightly according to the sacred law (*vrata*);
he who honors their law with hymns of praise, he who adorns the law with songs of praise.
Homage to the lofty Heaven, to the two worlds, to Mitra, and to the bounteous Varuṇa, the compassionate and bounteous one!
Praise Indra and Agni; praise the celestial Aryaman and Bhaga.
Living long, may we be united with progeny; may we be united with the protection of Soma.
Through the protection of the gods, may we, accompanied by Indra and sharing our own glory with the Maruts, be esteemed.
May Agni, Mitra, and Varuṇa grant us shelter; may we and the patrons attain that.
We have pressed [the juice] for you; come hither with the stones! These exhilarating Soma-draughts are mixed with milk, these exhilarating Soma-draughts.
O two Kings who touch the heavens, come to us, come near to us!
These bright Soma-draughts, mixed with milk, are for you both, O Mitra and Varuṇa; these bright Soma-draughts are mixed with milk.

Come hither to these drops, O [Aśvins], these pressed Soma juices mixed with curds, these pressed juices mixed with curds. And at the awakening of the Dawn, together with the rays of the Sun, the juice has been pressed for you,
for Mitra and Varuṇa to drink— the lovely one, for the sake of the Truth to drink.
Like a cow that yields milk at dawn, they milk that stalk for you with the stones; they milk the Soma with the stones. Come toward us, come hither to us, both of you, to drink the Soma!
O Mitra and Varuṇa, this Soma has been pressed by the men for you; it is pressed for your drinking.
On and on is the greatness of Pūṣan, the one of mighty birth, proclaimed; the praise of this powerful one does not weary, his hymn of praise does not weary.
Seeking favor, I sing to him who brings aid at hand, the source of bliss—he who, as a vigorous god, has drawn to himself the mind of every man, the vigorous god who has drawn it to himself.
For I urge you forward, O Pūṣan, as one would a swift steed on its path, with hymns of praise so that you may overcome our adversaries; like a camel, carry us across our adversaries.
Since I, a mortal, invoke you, the bliss-bestowing god, for friendship, make our songs of praise resplendent; in the contests for booty, make them resplendent.
O Pūṣan, those who are skilled in praise, being wise through their insight, have enjoyed the protection of your friendship; indeed, they have enjoyed it through your insight.
Following that most recent team of horses, we seek you for wealth.
O you of wide renown, do not be angry; be swift in every contest for booty; be swift in every contest for booty.
O Lord of the Unborn Steeds, be with us for our gain; do not be angry, but be a liberal giver to those who seek glory, O Lord of the Unborn Steeds!
O Wondrous One, may we turn you hither with excellent hymns of praise.
For I do not disregard you, O glowing Pūṣan; I do not deny your friendship.

Let there be *śrauṣaṭ*! With my thought, I place Agni at the forefront; now we choose that divine host, we choose Indra and Vāyu. Since this newest [hymn] has been offered at the navel of Vivasvat while he is active, may our prayers go forth toward the gods, even as our prayers do.
O Mitra and Varuṇa, when you two took that untruth away from the Truth by your own will, by your own will of skill;
then indeed in your dwellings we beheld the golden [soma],
through our prayers, through the mind, through our own eyes, through the own eyes of Soma.

O Aśvins, those seeking the gods invoke you with hymns of praise, like Āyus raising a cry; the Āyus call upon you for their oblations. O possessors of all wealth, all glories and nourishments rest upon you both.
O wonder-workers, the fellies of your golden chariot sprinkle moisture, your golden chariot.

O wonder-workers, you have been perceived; you open up the firmament. For you, in the rites of worship, they harness the chariot-steeds that are free from dust, in the rites of worship. O wonder-workers, we place you upon the seat of the golden chariot.
Like two travelers on a path, you traverse the mid-air, directing it straight, directing the mid-air.
O you two who possess power through your powers, favor us by day and by night! May your bounty never fail us; may your bounty never fail us at any time.
O bull-like Indra, these Soma drops, drunk by the bull, have been pressed; they are pressed by the stones, bursting forth—pressed for you, bursting forth.
May they exhilarate you for the sake of giving great and wondrous bounty.
O you who are borne by songs, being praised with hymns, come hither; as one who is most gracious, come to us.
O Agni, hear us! Being praised, you shall speak to the worshipful gods, to the worshipful kings.
Since you, O gods, gave that cow to the Aṅgirases, Aryaman milks her along with the fashioner; he knows her well along with me.
May those manly deeds of yours never turn away from us; may your ancient glories not decay, nor may they decay before our time.
Whatever wondrous, immortal, and ever-new sound you have produced age after age—O Maruts, bestow that upon us, and whatever is difficult to overcome, grant that which is difficult to overcome.

Dadhyañc, the ancient Aṅgiras, Priyamedha, Kaṇva, Atri, and Manu—these my ancestors know [this]; Manu knows them. Their lineage extends to the gods; our kinships are with them. Following their path, I bow down with my song; to Indra and Agni, I bow down with my song.
Let the Hotṛ sacrifice; let the seekers win what is desirable. Bṛhaspati, the seer, sacrifices with bulls—bulls rich in many boons.
We have ourselves grasped the far-reaching song of praise from the pressing-stone.
The one of noble will has established the non-giving ones; the one of noble will has established many dwellings.
O gods who are eleven in heaven, who are eleven upon the earth,
and who are eleven dwelling in the waters by your greatness— O gods, may you graciously accept this sacrifice.
To Agni, who sits upon the altar, whose abode is dear, and who shines with brilliant luster—bring forth a dwelling-place for him as one brings a nourishing draught.
Clothe the pure one, whose chariot is light, with bright color and who dispels the darkness, with a hymn as if with a garment.
The twice-born one speeds toward the threefold food; what was consumed grows strong again within the year.
With the tongue of one he is a noble bull, and with the other, the elephant-like one strips away the trees.
Moving through the darkness, his two co-dwelling mothers tremble; both cross over toward their infant.
With forward-pointing tongue, scattering [the mist] and dripping with thirst, he is to be approached—the one who stirs the waters, the strengthener of his father.
Seeking to release themselves for the sake of Manu, who acts like a man, the swift-running, black-tracked,
and impetuous steeds— unequalled, agile, lightly gliding, wind-impelled, and fleet— are harnessed.
Then his [flames], scattering [the darkness], move at will, making the black monster their great form;
when he has grasped the vast earth, he goes along panting, thundering, and roaring.
Adorning himself, he bends down over the brown [mares]; bellowing loudly, he approaches them like a bull his wives.
Displaying his vigor, he beautifies his own body; like a terrifying beast, he brandishes his horns, difficult to seize.
He, the pervasive one, the all-pervading, gathers them together; knowing them as his own kin, he rests eternally among those who know him.
They grow again and attain divinity; together with their parents, they assume another form.

The long-haired maidens, having been dead, stood up again for the sake of the living man, crying out together. Releasing them from old age, he goes along roaring, generating a supreme life-force, a living and unconquerable spirit.
Licking the upper garment of his mother, he indeed goes forth across the expanse with his powerful, bold warriors.
Bestowing vigor upon all that has feet, licking them evermore, the falcon-like one indeed follows along his paths.
O Agni, shine among our patrons; like a snorting bull, you are the domestic lord.
You have caused the mother-cows with their calves to glow, flickering all around like a coat of mail in battles.
O Agni, may this well-composed prayer be dearer to you than a poorly composed one, even more so than a beloved thought.
With that pure, bright radiance of your body which shines forth, do you win for us wealth.
O Agni, grant for our chariot and for our house a boat with constant oars and feet;
a boat that shall carry across our heroes, our wealthy patrons, and our people, and which shall be our protection.
O Agni, may you graciously accept our hymn; may Heaven and Earth and the self-praising Rivers grant it favor.
Seeking cattle and grain for a long life, may the ruddy ones bestow upon us our choice boon.
Truly, that beautiful splendor of the god has been established for the sake of majesty, since he was born from strength;
when he inclines toward it, the prayer succeeds, and the flowing streams of Truth have led him forward.
The nourishing, wondrous form, full of food, dwells eternally; a second [form] among the seven auspicious mothers.
For the milking of this bull, the young women have brought forth a third [form], the one who possesses tenfold wisdom.
When the wise lords, by their power, brought him forth from the depths with the form of the Great Steer;
when Mātariśvan churned him who was hidden in secret for the sake of the distillation of honey, following the ancient ways of the fathers.
When he is led forth from his father’s highest [abode], he rises wondrously upon the nourishing plants;
when both parents impel his birth, then the youngest one becomes pure with fervor.
Then he entered the mothers, in whom the pure one, remaining unhurt, grew wide;
when he had climbed up after the former ones that were born of old, he runs down among the newer, lower ones.
Then indeed they choose him as the Hotṛ-priest in the sacrifices for heaven; seeking fulfillment, they strive toward him as if toward Bhaga.
When, praised by many, he moves through the gods with wisdom and power, he goes everywhere to the mortal who offers praise, so that he may provide sustenance.
When he, the worshipful one, urged by the wind, has spread himself out like a restless, flickering flame that is never exhausted,
then on the flight of him who is burning, whose path is black, who is born of purity, the dust is stirred along his way.
Like a chariot that has gone forth, fashioned by skillful craftsmen, he speeds toward heaven with his ruddy limbs;
then those black drops of his, O Dakṣi, become brilliant rays, and from their brilliance, like the onset of a hero, the birds fly away.
For by you, O Agni, Varuṇa whose vows are firm, Mitra, and the bounteous Aryaman have been made strong;
since you, all-pervading, were born encompassing them on every side with your power, as the felly encompasses the spokes.
O Agni, youngest god, you bestow wealth and the assembly of deities upon the one who exerts himself and presses the soma;
as such, O youthful son of strength, we now establish you, the possessor of great wealth, like Bhaga in our song of praise.

Grant us wealth that is self-sustaining and domestic, like Bhaga and Dakṣa; grant us that which is enduring. Like reins, he who controls both worlds, the one of excellent wisdom, brings the praise of the gods under the Law (Ṛta).
Moreover, may the Hotṛ of bright luster, with swift horses, the delightful one with the shining chariot, hear us.
May that unerring Agni lead us by the best paths toward desirable wealth, prosperity, and greater well-being.
Agni has been praised with powerful hymns, establishing us further for sovereign rule.
May both those patrons and we ourselves spread abroad, as the sun drives away the mist.
O Agni, kindled, bring the gods today to the one who extends the ladle;
spin out the ancient thread for the donor who has pressed the soma.
O Tanūnapāt, you measure out for me the sacrifice rich in ghee and full of sweetness,
belonging to an inspired singer like me, who is diligent and offers oblations.
Pure, purifying, and wonderful, he sprinkles the sacrifice with honey;
Narāśaṃsa, the god worthy of worship among the gods, thrice [comes] from heaven.
O Agni, being praised, bring hither Indra— the wondrous, the beloved—
for this hymn of mine, O fair-tongued one, is directed toward you.
Spreading the sacrificial grass while holding out the ladles at the well-performed sacrifice,
I prepare for Indra a wide-extending shelter that provides the most ample space for the gods.
May the great divine doors, increasers of cosmic order, pure, much-desired, and unfailing, open wide for the gods to advance.
May Night and Dawn, the two neighboring goddesses who are praised, well-adorned, the mighty mothers of Cosmic Order (Ṛta), sit down upon the sacrificial grass with favor.
May the two divine Hotṛ-priests, the sages with lovely tongues who are ever-praising,
perform for us today this successful sacrifice that reaches the heavens.
Pure among the gods, Hotrā is established among the Maruts; may Bhāratī, Iḷā, Sarasvatī, and Mahī sit upon the sacrificial grass, they who are worthy of worship.
May Tvaṣṭṛ, who is well-disposed toward us, release for our prosperity and wealth that wondrous seed of ours— abundant, manifold in itself, and rich in boons— at our very center.
Releasing [the offerings] by yourself, O Vanaspati, sacrifice to the gods;
Agni, the wise god among the gods, prepares the oblations well.
To Vāyu, who is accompanied by Pūṣan and the Maruts, and by all the gods— to Indra, who is stirred by the Gāyatrī, offer the oblation with the cry of Svāhā!
Come to the offerings consecrated with *svāhā* to partake of them;
O Indra, come, hear our call, for they invoke you at the sacrifice.

I bring forward a more powerful, newer prayer for Agni; I offer a word and a hymn to the Son of Strength, he who is the beloved grandson of the Waters, the Hotṛ-priest who has sat down upon the earth in due season along with the Vasus.
Being born in the highest heaven, Agni became manifest to Mātariśvan. By the power and the greatness of him as he was kindled, his flame caused both Heaven and Earth to shine forth.

His flames are brilliant and ageless; his rays are beautiful to behold, from him whose face is fair and whose luster is excellent. With their radiant power, O Agni, they quiver like rivers across the night, unceasing and undecaying.
Him whom the Bhṛgus have sent forth—the all-knowing one—at the navel of the earth, by the greatness of the world;
that Agni, do thou urge on with songs in your own home, he who alone rules over wealth like Varuṇa.

He whom no one can restrain, like the roar of the Maruts, like an army set in motion, or like a celestial thunderbolt—Agni eats and chews with his sharp jaws; like a warrior against his enemies, he overcomes the forests.
Will Agni indeed be the hero of our hymn? Will the Vasu, together with the Vasus, fulfill our desire?
Will he, the impeller, truly speed our prayers toward their attainment? Him of the radiant countenance, I praise with this prayer.
With ghee as his face, Agni sits at the pole of the Cosmic Order (ṛta); like a friend, he is approached by one who kindles him.
Kindling him, the singer shines resplendent in the assemblies; may he lift up our prayer, bright-colored and upward-tending.
O Agni, with your unfailing, auspicious, and powerful guardians, protect us;
with those that are undeceived, undaunted, and unwinking, O Desired One, guard our offspring on every side.
The Hotṛ goes forth to his office by his wondrous power, holding aloft the pure-hued prayer;
he moves toward the ladles turned to the right, which first kiss his station.
The milking-streams of the Eternal Order have lowed toward him, encompassed within the womb, in the seat of the god;
when he dwelt distributed in the lap of the waters, he then sucked the self-sustaining powers by which he moves.
Desiring to win that same wondrous prize together, two of equal age strive against one another for the common goal;
then, like Bhaga, he is to be invoked by us, and like a charioteer, he has gathered the reins of the draft-horses.

Him whom two of equal age revere, a pair dwelling together in the same womb and the same abode—he, the grey-haired, was born as a youth, both by day and by night; ageless, he moves through many human generations.
The ten fingers and our prayers impel him; we mortals call upon the god for aid.
From the dry land he speeds down the slope; with those who follow him, he has established new paths.
For you, O Agni, rule over that which is celestial; you, by your own self, are the guardian of that which is terrestrial, like a herdsman.
These two great, shimmering, golden, and winding ones, rich in splendor, have settled upon the sacred grass.
O Agni, graciously accept and delight in this word, O joyous one, self-sustained, born of Truth, and of noble power—
you who face every direction, who are beautiful to behold, delightful to look upon, like a dwelling-place full of nourishment.
Ask him; he has gone there. He knows it; as one who perceives, he moves forward; indeed, he moves along that path.
In him are the commands; in him are the sacrifices. He is the lord of the powerful strength of the prize-winning steed.

They ask him, yet he does not question them; for what he has grasped with his own wise mind, he does not forget, neither the first word nor the later one. Undeluded, he acts in accordance with his will.
To him indeed go the sacrificial ladles; to him go the mares. He alone shall hear all my words.
Having many commands, the overcomer, the accomplisher of sacrifice, the one of unbroken protection, the infant has assumed his vigorous strength.
When he has come together and moves about as one to be attended upon, as soon as born he hastens with his companions.
He touches the glowing heat for joy and delight, when the longing ones approach him who stands firm.
Like a wild beast of the waters or a forest-roamer, he has been laid down upon the highest skin.
Agni, the wise one who knows the *ṛta* and is true, has proclaimed the ways to mortals.
I praise Agni, the three-headed and seven-rayed, who is never-failing in the lap of his parents; he sits within this moving yet firm world, having filled all the luminous realms of heaven.
The great bull has grown toward these two; undecaying and far-reaching, he stands with his protection.
He plants his feet upon the ridges of the wide earth; his ruddy flames lick the udder.
Moving toward their common calf, the two well-fashioned milch-cows wander in all directions;
unceasingly measuring out their paths, they bestow all great insights upon the world.
The wise poets lead him to his station; guarding with various hearts the one who does not age, they looked all around, desiring to win the river. Sūrya became manifest to them, to the men.
Worthy to be beheld, victorious throughout the quarters, to be invoked for the great and the small so that they may live—
since he has become visible in many places through the days, the bounteous one is all-visible to these embryos.
How, O Agni, have those who purify themselves offered to you with the strength of Ayu, aspiring for booty?
When the gods, establishing both seed and progeny, took delight in the harmony of the Eternal Order (ṛta).
O youngest one, self-sustained lord, take heed of this my speech, which is most bountiful and offered to you.
One person reviles, while another praises; I, your worshipper, laud your very body, O Agni.

Those guardians of yours, O Agni, who, seeing him blind, protected Māmateya from misfortune—they, the all-knowing one, protected those doers of good; though the enemies sought to deceive them, they did not succeed in deceiving them.
O Agni, whoever is stingy toward us, malicious, and hostile, who harms us with duplicity—may that heavy spell recoil upon him; may he destroy his own body with his evil words.

Or rather, O Victorious One, whatever mortal harms another mortal through duplicity, though he be well-informed—protect the one who praises you from that, O Agni; while being praised yourself, do not deliver us to misfortune.
When Mātariśvan, having entered it, stirred him— the Hotṛ priest who belongs to all waters and all gods—
him whom they established among the human clans, bright like the sun, resplendent for the sake of beauty.
Let them not deceive the one who offers prayers; may Agni take pleasure in my protection.
May they enjoy all his deeds and the praise of the poet who brings the offering.
Him whom the worshipful ones have seized in his eternal dwelling and established with praises;
they lead him forward, grasping him in the sacrifice like swift horses of a chariot that hasten on.
The wondrous one destroys many things with his jaws; then, radiant, he shines within the forest.
Then the wind blows after his flame day after day, like the arrow of an archer shot at its mark.
Him, while still in the womb, neither enemies nor those seeking to harm can injure with their assaults;
blind and sightless, they cannot deceive him by their gaze; his own eternal protectors have guarded him.
He, the lord of the house, seeks great wealth; he stands at the station of powerful riches.
The pressing-stones attend him as he hastens toward us.
He who is the bull among men, as [he is] for the two worlds (Heaven and Earth), whose flow is drunk by the living through his glories— he who, having sped forth, has settled in his place of origin.
He who has illuminated the city Nārmiṇī, like a courser, a seer, like a steed of the clouds;
shining like the sun, he whose self is a hundredfold.
The doubly-born one, blazing brightly, has taken his stand over the three luminous realms and all the regions,
the most excellent sacrificer, in the gathering place of the waters.
This is that Hotṛ priest who, having a twofold birth, possesses all desirable things for the sake of glory—
he, the mortal, who has offered oblations to him with well-prepared gifts.
O Agni, as a liberal donor I have called upon you many times; for you, indeed, are like the protection of a great impeller.
Even at the sacrifice of one who is wealthy yet lacks breath,
or of one who is stingy and godless, may he never depart.
O Agni, that mortal who is brilliant, wise, great, and most exalted in heaven— may we, as thy worshippers, ever advance before him.

Him whom those seeking cattle, with skillful thought, have generated at the sacrifice among the waters like a friend for the sake of the rite—the two worlds trembled before his splendor and his song; he is the beloved, the worshipful one, the protector of all beings.
When those [deeds] of yours for the Soma-presser Purumīḷha were established, like friends, by the self-sustaining ones;
then you two found the will and the path for the singer—O Bulls, hear the call of the one who dwells in his home.
The peoples have honored your birth from the two worlds, O Bulls, for it is to be proclaimed for great skill;
when you bring [the oblation] for the sake of *ṛta* and for the steed, you enjoy the sacrifice through the invocation and the ritual labor.
That people is indeed great, O Asuras, which you two, observers of *ṛta*, proclaim as the mighty *ṛta*.
You two harness the active skill of lofty heaven to the waters, as one yokes a cow to the pole.
In this great rite, you two fulfill the desire by your greatness; the dustless, impetuous milch-cows sit in the dwelling.
They low toward the sun at its setting and at the break of dawn, like swift birds.
The long-haired maidens have sung out for you both according to the Eternal Law (*ṛta*), O Mitra and Varuṇa, where you celebrate the path.
By your own selves, release [the waters] and cause our prayers to swell; you two rule over the inspired thoughts of the sage.

Whosoever, striving with sacrifices, offers worship to you both—the sage who as the Hotṛ-priest performs the sacrifice, accomplishing the prayer—unto him you two indeed come; you enjoy the ritual and approach our songs with favor, being well-disposed toward us.
You two, the upholders of *ṛta*, are first anointed by sacrifices and with cows at the employment of the mind, as it were.
They bring you songs of praise with concentrated thought; with an undeluded mind, you have attained wealth.
O Heroes, you bestow wealthy vigor; with your wondrous powers you have attained wealth and great protection from here.
Neither the heavens with their days, nor the rivers, nor the Paṇis have attained your divinity or your bounty.

You two clothe yourselves in fat garments; your thoughts are flawless, indeed like continuous streams. You have struck down all falsehoods; O Mitra and Varuṇa, you are united with the cosmic order (*ṛta*).
Not even one among them has clearly understood this: the true mantra, proclaimed by the seers, is powerful and fierce.
The four-edged, terrible [thunderbolt] strikes the three-edged; thus the first revilers of the gods have been worn away.
The footless one comes first among those that have feet; who, O Mitra and Varuṇa, understands this of yours?
The embryo bears its burden even as it is born; it fulfills the *ṛta* and overcomes the *anṛta*.
We behold him as he moves away from the maidens like a lover, never falling down; he clothes himself in wide-spreading, impenetrable garments—the beloved domain of Mitra and Varuṇa.
Born without a horse, without a rein, the steed neighs loudly as he flies with his back uplifted.
The youths have delighted in the thoughtless prayer, praising the foundation established in Mitra and Varuṇa.
May the milch-cows, who favor the son of Mamatā, cause him who loves the sacred word (*brahman*) to swell at this very udder.
Knowing the ways, let him beg for food; seeking [it] with his mouth, he shall win over Aditi.

O gods Mitra and Varuṇa, may I turn you both toward the enjoyment of our oblation with reverence and for your protection. May our sacred prayer be victorious in battles; may we have divine rain that brings us safely across.
We worship you two, the great ones, with offerings and salutations, O Mitra and Varuṇa, being of one accord—
O you who drip with ghee— with ghee, since the Adhvaryus bring [the oblations] to you through our prayers as it were for us.
O Mitra and Varuṇa, this well-fashioned hymn is offered to you as a presentation, like a ritual act;
for the Hotṛ priest anoints you both at the assemblies, and the patron, seeking to win your favor, O mighty ones, desires your goodwill.
The cow Aditi has swelled with milk for the one who acts according to the *ṛta*, for the person who offers the oblation, O Mitra and Varuṇa.
When he serves you in the assembly, honoring you, that man becomes like a human *hotṛ* priest who has presented the oblation.
Moreover, among the exhilarating clans, may the cows and the divine waters cause the soma-juice to swell for you both.
And so, O ancient Lord of the house, enjoy this; drink of the milk of the ruddy cow.
I shall now proclaim the heroic deeds of Viṣṇu, who measured out the earthly regions;
he who, striding in three steps, the wide-strider, propped up the highest dwelling place.
For that heroic deed Viṣṇu is praised, like a terrifying beast, roaming and dwelling in the mountains;
he in whose three wide strides all the worlds abide.
Let this hymn go forth as strength for Viṣṇu, the bull who dwells in the mountains and strides widely—
he who alone measured out this long, extended common dwelling-place with three steps.
He whose three steps, filled with honey, rejoice in imperishable self-sustenance;
he who alone has supported the threefold earth and the sky, and all existing beings.
May I attain that beloved domain of his where men devoted to the gods rejoice;
for there, in the highest footstep of Viṣṇu, the wide-striding one, is the kinsman and the fountain of honey.
We desire to go to those dwellings of yours where the many-horned, tireless cows abide. There, indeed, the supreme station of the wide-striding bull shines forth abundantly.
Sing forth with prayer to your great hero Viṣṇu, who is mindful of the pressed juice,
and to him who dwells upon the ridges of the mountains, the two undeceivable ones who stand like a noble steed.
Truly, the brilliant encounter of you two, the impetuous ones, O Indra and Viṣṇu, protects the drinker of the pressed juice;
for you ward off the missile of the archer Kṛśānu that is aimed at a mortal.
These [streams] increase his great manly power; he brings down the two parents for the sake of seed and enjoyment.
The son establishes the lower and the higher name of the father, and a third name in the luminous realm of heaven.
We celebrate each of those manly deeds of his— the protector, the harmless,
the bounteous— who with three strides traversed the earthly realms for the wide-striding one to live in spacious freedom.
Two indeed are the strides of him who beholds the light; having gazed upon them, the mortal stirs himself. No one dares to approach his third stride, not even the winged birds as they fly.
Together with the ninety-four names, he has set the wheel in motion like a revolving disc;
the youth, large-bodied and measured out by the singers, returns to the battle-cry.

May you be gracious like Mitra, fed with clarified butter, possessing far-reaching splendor, swift-moving, and wide-extending. Therefore, O Viṣṇu, even by the wise your praise is to be perfected, and your sacrifice is to be accomplished by the one who offers oblations.
He who offers worship to Viṣṇu— the ancient, most recent ordainer,
the one who possesses excellent glory— and he who proclaims the great birth of this Great One, shall indeed surpass even his equal through his glories.
O singers, fulfill him from his very birth as the ancient germ of *ṛta*, according to your knowledge;
knowing even his names, proclaim them. O Viṣṇu, may we partake of your great favor.
King Varuṇa, the two Aśvins, and the Maruts, the wise ones, attend to this will of his, the ordainer.
Viṣṇu, possessing the highest skill and knowledge of the days, maintains the power; together with his friend, he opens the stall.

Viṣṇu, the divine ordainer who has come for companionship, most skillful in action for the sake of the well-doing Indra— established in his three abodes, he has quickened the Ārya and granted the sacrificer a share in the portion of the Eternal Order (Ṛta).
Agni has been awakened; Sūrya rises from the earth; the radiant Dawn has shone forth with her great beam.
The Aśvins have yoked their chariot to travel; the god Savitṛ has impelled every moving creature apart.
When you two, O Aśvins, harness your bull-like chariot, sprinkle our dominion with ghee and honey;
quicken our sacred prayer in battles, and may we share in the spoils in the contest for booty.
May the well-praised chariot of the Aśvins come hither—three-wheeled, carrying honey, drawn by swift horses;
may that three-seated, wealthy vehicle, possessing all prosperity, bring welfare to our bipeds and quadrupeds.
O Aśvins, bring nourishment to us; sprinkle us with your honeyed whip.
Prolong our lives, wipe away our sins, drive off our enemies, and be our companions.
You two place the embryo within moving creatures; you two are within all existing beings. O Aśvins, you two, the bulls, have set in motion Agni, the waters, and the lords of the forest.
You two indeed are physicians with your remedies; moreover, you are charioteers with your skill in driving.
Furthermore, O fierce ones, you bestow sovereign power upon that man who, possessing oblations, serves you with his mind.
O Vasus and Rudras, you of many counsels, increasing in strength, O mighty ones, grant us your favor in our desire!
For you, O wonder-workers, when Ucathya sought wealth from you, you hastened forth with your ungrudging aids.

Who may offer worship to you both for this very favor, O Vasus, since you bestow it through homage at the station of the Cow? Awaken for us wealthy inspirations, as you two move with a mind that fulfills every desire.
When your powerful protector was harnessed for the son of Tugra, he was established in the midst of the surging flood;
may I come unto your protection and refuge, as a hero hastens to the fray with flying strides.
May Upastuti protect me from the son of Ucathya; may these two winged ones not suck me dry.
Let not the ten-fold piled fuel consume me, when, bound for you both, it devours the earth itself.
The rivers, most motherly, did not swallow me up when the Dāsas cast me down while I was tightly bound.
When Traitana hewed away his head, the Dāsa himself gnawed upon his own breast and shoulders.
Dīrghatamas, son of Mamatā, having grown old in the tenth age,
becomes the Brahman-priest and the charioteer of the waters as they go toward their goal.
I praise with sacrifices at the assemblies the two great ones, Heaven and Earth, who increase the cosmic order (*ṛta*) and are wise;
they who, sons of the gods, together with the gods, perform wondrous deeds and bestow desirable boons through their excellent wisdom.
And I think of the mind of the guileless Father and the great inherent power of the Mother;
through their invocations, the two parents of noble seed have made the world wide for progeny, and through their vastness, they have established immortality.
Those sons, skillful in their work and wondrous in their deeds, brought forth the two great parents for the sake of primordial awareness.
You two guard the station of the son who is free from duplicity, according to the true law of all that is stationary and all that moves.
Those wise magicians, the twins of common origin and shared dwelling, have measured out their course;
the radiant sages weave a new thread after new one in the sky, within the ocean.
Today we meditate upon that desirable gift of Savitṛ at the impulse of the god.
O Heaven and Earth, with your benevolent mind, bestow upon us wealth abounding in goods and consisting of hundreds of cattle.
For they, Heaven and Earth, are the benefactors of all, observers of cosmic order (*ṛta*), and the sustainers of the realm, wise seers.
Between these two divine powers of noble birth, the pure god Sūrya moves according to the eternal law (*dharman*).
The wide-extending, mighty, and inexhaustible Father and Mother protect all beings;
the two worlds are most courageous and beautiful, since the Father has clothed them in forms.
He, the wise son of his two parents, the bearer of oblations, purifies the worlds by his creative power;
from the dappled cow and the bull of excellent seed, he milks for all days the bright milk of this [soma].

This one is the most skillful worker among the skillful gods, who brought forth the two worlds that are auspicious to all; he, the wise one, measured out the two regions and has firmly established them with unaging supports.
O Heaven and Earth, being praised by us, you two of great power, bestow upon us great glory and lofty dominion;
with that [power] may we always overcome the peoples, and do you both instill in us praiseworthy might.

What has the eldest come to us? What has the youngest? What mission does he perform as messenger, and what have we said? We have not reviled the cup which is of noble lineage; O Agni, brother, we have indeed praised the excellence of the wooden vessel.

"Make the single chalice into four," so the gods said to you; that is what I have come to tell you. O sons of Sudhanvan, if you will do exactly this, you shall become worthy of sacrifice together with the gods.
When you spoke to Agni the messenger, saying, "A horse must be made, and a chariot must be made here;
a milch-cow must be made, and two youths must be made"—O brothers, we approach you having performed those very deeds.
Having performed that deed, O Ṛbhus, you asked: "Where has he gone who came to us as a messenger?
When Tvaṣṭar saw the four cups made, he hid himself among the divine women.
"Let us slay them," so Tvaṣṭṛ said, "those who have reviled the cup from which the gods drink. They assume other names at the pressing; with other names the maiden has wedded them.
Indra yoked his two bay horses; the Aśvins [yoked] their chariot; Bṛhaspati brought the multiform [cow].
As Ṛbhu, Vibhvan, and Vāja, you went to the gods; as skillful workers, you obtained your share of the sacrifice.
From the hide you brought forth the cow by means of your insights; you who were old, you made yourselves young again.
O sons of Sudhanvan, you fashioned horse after horse from a horse; having yoked the chariot, you went unto the gods.
"Drink this water," you said; "or rather, drink this water used for washing the *muñja* grass.
O sons of Sudhanvan, if you do not find pleasure in that, then indeed you shall rejoice at the third libation.
"The waters are most abundant," said one; "Agni is most abundant," said another.
One proclaimed her who is being carried away for many. Speaking the Truth, you fashioned the cups.
One drives away the lame cow that drinks no water; another carves the meat brought on the carving-board.
One carries away the dung before sunset; what indeed did the two parents do for their sons?
On the heights you made grass for him, and in the valleys, by your skillful work, O heroes, you made water.
Since you lay down in the house of Agohya, O Ṛbhus, you do not follow after that which is here today.
When you crept around the worlds with eyes closed, where indeed were your two dear parents then?
You cursed him who seized your foreleg; to him who spoke out against you, you cried back in reply.
When you had fallen asleep, O Ṛbhus, you asked this: "O Agohya, who has awakened us here?
The goat declared the dog to be the awakener; today, after a full year, he has opened his eyes.
By day the Maruts go; Agni goes upon the earth; this Vāta goes through the mid-air;
Varuṇa goes with the waters and the oceans, seeking you, O sons of strength.
May Mitra, Varuṇa, Aryaman, Āyu, Indra, Ṛbhukṣan, and the Maruts not look with disdain upon us,
as we proclaim in the assembly the heroic deeds of the vigorous steed, born of the gods.
When they lead forth from his mouth the seized offering of the goat, who is covered with a bright garment and wealth,
the bleating, multiform goat goes straight forward to the beloved path of Indra and Pūṣan.
This goat, the portion for Pūṣan, belonging to all the gods, is led before the vigorous horse;
since Tvaṣṭṛ quickens this beloved sacrificial cake (puroḍāśa) together with the steed for the sake of glorious renown.
When men lead the horse, fit for oblation, three times around the path that leads to the gods according to the seasons,
there the goat, Pūṣan’s first portion, goes forth, announcing the sacrifice to the gods.
The Hotṛ, the Adhvaryu, the Āvayāj, the Agnimindha, the Grāvagrābha, and the wise Śaṃstṛ—
with this well-prepared and well-offered sacrifice, fill the channels of the belly.

May those who hew the sacrificial post, those who carry the post, and those who carve the *caṣāla* for the horse’s post, as well as those who prepare the cooking-vessel for the steed— may the approval of all these impel us forward.
He has come near; my prayer has been well-established for me. He of the smooth back has approached the quarters of the gods.
The inspired seers rejoice after him; we have made him a good kinsman in the prosperity of the gods.
Whatever halter or tether belongs to the prize-winning steed, whatever head-stall, girth, or rope he has,
or whatever grass is placed in his mouth as fodder— may all those things of yours be among the gods.
Whatever of the horse’s raw flesh the fly has eaten, or whatever remains smeared on the sacrificial post or the axe,
whatever is on the hands of the slaughterer or on his nails— may all of that be yours among the gods.
Whatever undigested contents of the belly escape, and whatever odor there is of raw flesh,
let the immolators make that well-prepared, and let them cook the sacrificial meat thoroughly done.

Whatever from your body, as it is being cooked by fire, drips down toward the spit when you have been impaled—let that not rest upon the earth, nor upon the grass; let it be granted to the longing gods.
Those who look upon the horse as cooked, those who say, "It smells good,
take it away," and those who wait for a portion of the steed's flesh— may even their approval further us.
The inspection of the flesh-cooking cauldron, the vessels for pouring the broth,
the warming covers for the pots, the hooks, and the carving-boards— all these attend upon the horse.
The stepping forth, the sitting down, the rolling over, and the tethering-rope of the horse;
that which he drank and that which he ate as fodder—may all those of yours be among the gods.

Let not the smoke-scented fire crackle at you, nor let the glowing cauldron, smelling of its contents, burst asunder. O gods, accept this horse—sacrificed, welcomed, approved, and consecrated with the cry of *vaṣaṭ*.
The garment they spread beneath the horse, the upper covering, the golden ornaments, the halter, and the foot-rope— these dear things they offer to the steed among the gods.
Whatever of yours was pained while sitting, by the great [blow], or by the heel, or by the whip—
just as one offers the oblation with a ladle at the sacrifices, all those I heal for you with a sacred prayer (*brahman*).
The axe meets the thirty-four ribs of the horse, the steed of the friend of the gods.
Make its limbs free from injury; following the joints, proclaiming them one by one, dissect it according to the proper rules.
One is the dissector of Tvaṣṭṛ’s horse; two are the restrainers, and such is the season.
Those limbs of yours which I prepare in due order, those I offer as balls of flesh into the fire.
Let not your dear self burn you as you enter it; let not the axe linger upon your body.
Let not the greedy, unskilled dissector, passing over the vulnerable spots, mangle your limbs falsely with the knife.
Verily, you do not die here, nor do you suffer harm; you go to the gods by easy paths.
Your two bay steeds have become spotted deer; the vigorous steed has taken its place at the yoke of the donkey.
May the prize-winning steed grant us abundance of cattle, abundance of horses, male offspring, and wealth that nourishes all;
may Aditi grant us sinlessness, and may the horse, accompanied by oblations, win for us sovereign power.
When you first neighed at birth, rising from the ocean or from the primordial waters,
with the wings of a hawk and the forelegs of a deer— great and worthy of praise was your birth, O steed.
Yama gave him; Trita harnessed him; Indra was the first to mount him. The Gandharva grasped his rein; O Vasus, you fashioned the horse from the sun.
You are Yama; you are Āditya, O steed; you are Trita by your secret vow.
You are parted from Soma by an interval; they say you have three bonds in heaven.
They say you have three bonds in heaven, three in the waters, and three within the ocean.
O steed, may Varuṇa be gracious to me at that place where they say your highest birthplace is.
O powerful steed, these are your grooming-stations; these are the places where the hooves of the prize-winner are set down. Here I beheld your auspicious reins, which the guardians of *ṛta* protect.
I recognized you as yourself by means of my mind, like a bird flying down from heaven;
I beheld your head, the winged one, panting along easy paths that are free from dust.
Here I beheld thy supreme form, striving to win the food at the station of the cow;
when the mortal has provided enjoyment for thee, then, O most voracious one, thou hast swallowed up the plants.
After you, O steed, comes the chariot; after you, the young man; after you, the cows; after you, the fortune of maidens.
After you, the troops have sought your friendship; after you, the gods have measured out their heroic power.
Golden-horned, his feet were of iron; he was swift as thought, yet Indra was his superior.
The gods themselves came to eat his sacrificial food—he who was the first to mount the steed.
With broad flanks and slender waists, the divine coursers are like heroes;
like swans they fly in rows when the horses have reached the celestial racecourse.
O steed, your body is winged; your mind is swift-gliding like the wind.
Your horns are fixed in many places; they move flickeringly in the forests.
The vigorous steed has come to the place of instruction, meditating with a mind directed toward the gods.
The goat, his kin, is led before him; behind him follow the sages and the singers.
He has approached the highest dwelling place, the steed toward his father and mother;
for today he shall go to the gods as the most beloved, and then he shall bestow desirable gifts upon the donor.
Of this lovely, gray-haired Hotṛ-priest, his middle brother is Aśna;
his third brother has ghee upon his back. Here I beheld the Lord of the People, who has seven sons.
Seven yoke the one-wheeled chariot; a single horse draws it, having seven names.
Three-naved is the wheel, undecaying and invincible, upon which all these worlds rest.
Upon this seven-wheeled chariot stand the seven; seven horses draw it. Seven sisters sing together toward it, where the seven names of the cows are deposited.
Who has seen the first-born being born, when that which is boneless supports that which possesses bones?
Where indeed is the life-force, the breath, and the blood of the earth? Who has gone to one who knows this to ask about it?
As a simpleton, not understanding with my mind, I ask about these established footprints of the gods:
upon the yearling calf, the sages have stretched out seven threads to weave.
Unaware, I ask the wise seers here for the sake of knowledge, as one who does not know:
what indeed is that One in the form of the Unborn, by whom these six worlds were propped apart?
Let him who truly knows it speak here of this lovely bird’s hidden station;
from its head the cows milk forth milk, and wearing its covering, they have drunk the water with their feet.
The Mother distributed her portion to the Father according to the Eternal Law (*ṛta*); for in the beginning she united with him through thought and inspired vision.
She, loathing the essence of the embryo, was pierced; then those who offered homage approached her with their prayer.
The Mother was yoked to the pole of the sacrificial fee; the Embryo stood within the enclosures.
The Calf lowed as he beheld the Cow of manifold forms across the three distances.
Bearing three mothers and three fathers, he stands alone, erect; they do not weary him.
Upon the back of that heaven, they deliberate in speech that knows all things, yet does not move all.
The twelve-spoked wheel of *Ṛta* indeed revolves around the sky so as not to decay;
O Agni, thereon stand the sons in pairs—seven hundred and twenty.
They call the Father five-footed, twelve-formed, rich in moisture, in the further half of heaven;
but these others say he is the far-seeing one, set upon the seven-wheeled, six-spoked [chariot] below.
Upon the five-spoked wheel as it revolves, all beings rest; its axle, though bearing a heavy burden, does not grow hot, and from of old its nave has never been shattered.
The wheel with its rim, ageless, revolves; ten yoked [horses] carry it upon the outstretched [chariot].
The eye of Sūrya moves through the mid-air, enveloped; in it all beings are fixed.
Of those born together, they say the seventh was born alone; these six are the twin seers, born of the gods.
Their desired offerings are established according to their stations; for the Sustainer, they tremble, transformed according to their forms.

What are female, those they call male to me; he who has eyes sees them, yet the blind does not discern them. The son who is a seer perceives them; he who understands them shall be the father of his father.
Beneath the higher realm and beyond this lower one, the Cow has risen up, bearing her calf with her foot.
Whitherward has she gone? To which region has she departed? Where indeed will she give birth? For she is not within the herd.

Who here can declare it, acting like a seer—what god was born from what source—that he who knows his father beyond this lower realm, or he who knows him below this higher realm? 1.164.18abc RV_1,164.18a avaḥ pareṇa pitaraṃ yo asyānuveda para enāvareṇa / RV_1,164.18c kavīyamānaḥ ka iha pra vocad devam manaḥ kuto adhi prajātam //
Those who go hitherward they call going away, and those who go away they call coming hither;
O Indra and Soma, those things which you two have fashioned carry them along the mid-air like yoked horses at the pole.
Two birds, inseparable companions, embrace the same tree. Of these two, one eats the sweet fruit, while the other looks on without eating.
Where the well-winged ones, never blinking, cry out together toward their share of immortality at the assemblies—
there the wise guardian of the entire world, the lord, has entered me, the simple one.
On that tree whereon all the fair-winged ones who eat honey settle and breed, they say its fruit is sweet at the top; he does not reach it who does not know the Father.
That which is the Gāyatra placed upon the Gāyatra, or that from which they fashioned the Triṣṭubh out of the Triṣṭubh,
or the Jagatī-foot placed within the Jagatī— those who know this have attained immortality.
With the *gāyatrī* he measures out the *arka*; with the *arka*, the *sāman* in the *triṣṭubh* meter; with the *vāka*, the *vāka*.
With the two-footed and four-footed syllable, they measure out the seven voices.
With the *jagatī* he propped up the ocean in heaven; with the *rathantara* he beheld the sun.
They say there are three kindling-sticks of the *gāyatrī*; from there it excels by its greatness and majesty.
I call hither this well-milking cow; may the skillful milker milk her.
May Savitar impel for us the most excellent impulse. The Gharma has been heated; that indeed I shall proclaim.
Muttering "hiṅ," the mistress of treasures has come hither, seeking her calf with her mind.
May this inviolable cow yield milk for the two Aśvins; may she prosper for our great good fortune.
The cow has lowed toward her blinking calf; she has made the "hiṅ" sound at his head to measure him.
Lowing toward the warm milk in her mouth, she utters her cry and yields her milk with her streams.

This is that which bellows, by which the cow is encompassed; she lows her lowing sound, resting upon the desert place. By her insights she has indeed humbled the mortal; becoming lightning, she cast off her covering.
The breathless one lies within the moving, living, and firm [body] in the midst of the dwellings.
The living spirit of the dead moves by means of its own powers; the immortal shares a common womb with the mortal.
I beheld the Herdsman, who never rests, moving hither and thither along his paths;
clothed in converging and diverging rays, he revolves repeatedly within the worlds.
He who made this does not know it; he who saw it is indeed far removed from it.
Enveloped within his mother’s womb, he who has many offspring has entered into destruction.
Heaven is my father, my progenitor; there is my navel. This great earth is my kin, my mother. Between the two upturned bowls lies the womb; therein the father deposited the seed within his daughter.
I ask you about the furthest limit of the earth; I ask where the navel of the world is.
I ask you about the seed of the stallion; I ask about the highest heaven of speech.
This altar is the furthest limit of the earth; this sacrifice is the navel of the world.
This Soma is the seed of the stallion; this Brahman is the highest heaven of speech.

Seven half-germs, the seed of the world, abide by the command of Viṣṇu in the established order; they, through their insights and their mind, being wise, as encompassers, surround all things on every side.
I do not discern what this is that I am; hidden and armored by the mind, I move about. When the first-born of Cosmic Order come to me, then indeed I obtain a share of this speech.
Moving away and moving toward, held by its own inherent power, the immortal one shares a common womb with the mortal.
These two, eternal and divergent, move apart; people perceive one, but they do not perceive the other.

In the imperishable syllable, in the highest heaven, upon which all the gods are seated—the Ṛg-verses—what will he do with the Ṛg-verse who does not know that? But those who know it, they sit together here.
O blessed one, may you indeed have abundant, good pasture; and may we also be blessed. Eat grass, O inviolable one, at all times; drink pure water as you wander.
The ruddy cow has lowed, fashioning the waters; she who is one-footed, two-footed, four-footed, eight-footed, and nine-footed, possessing a thousand syllables, dwells in the highest heaven.
From her the oceans flow forth; by her the four quarters of space live.
From her flows that imperishable [syllable], upon which the entire universe depends for life.
From afar, by means of the wind, I saw the smoke consisting of *śaka* rising above the lower [world].
The heroes cooked the speckled bull; these were the first ordinances.
Three long-haired ones appear in due season; one of them shears his hair within the year.
One beholds the universe with his powers; the speed of one is seen, but not his form.
Speech has been measured out in four quarters; those Brahmins who are wise know them.
Three, hidden in the cave, do not stir; the fourth quarter of speech is what humans speak.
They call him Indra, Mitra, Varuna, and Agni; and he is the divine, fair-winged Garutman.
That which is one, the sages call by many names; they call it Agni, Yama, and Matarishvan.
The tawny, well-winged birds fly up to heaven, clothed in the waters along their black path;
they have returned from the seat of Cosmic Order, and from them indeed the earth is moistened with clarified butter.
Twelve are the fellies, one the wheel, and three the naves; who indeed has understood that?
Into it thirty spokes are fixed together at once, sixty that are both moving and unmoving.

O Sarasvatī, that breast of yours which is inexhaustible, which is a source of bliss, by which you nourish all desirable things— that breast which bestows jewels, finds wealth, and grants good gifts— bring it here for him to suck.
With sacrifice the gods sacrificed to the sacrifice; those were the first ordinances. Those great ones attained the firmament where the ancient Sādhyas, the gods, abide.
This same water rises upward and flows downward through the days;
Parjanya quickens the earth, and the fires quicken the heavens.
The divine, well-winged, vast bird, the embryo of the waters, the beautiful one among the plants;
him who satisfies [the world] from all sides with rains, Sarasvant I invoke for protection.
By what auspicious power have the Maruts, of equal age and common dwelling, joined together as one?
With what intention have they come from where? From whence do these bulls roar their strength, seeking wealth?
Whose prayers have the youthful Maruts accepted? Who has turned them toward his sacrifice?
Like hawks gliding through the mid-air, by what great thought may we cause them to halt?

From where do you come alone, O Indra, the mighty one, O Lord of the Good? What is it thus that you ask as you encounter those who are radiant? Tell us that, O Lord of the Bay Horses, which is yours among us.
My sacred prayers and thoughts are for my welfare; the pressed juices and my strength stir within me; the pressing-stone is set forth for me.
They call out to you and long for you with their hymns; these two bay steeds carry you toward us.

Therefore, yoking ourselves with these closest companions, adorning our bodies with our own powers, we now harness these [steeds] with great splendors; for you, O Indra, have indeed come to us according to our own nature.
Where, O Maruts, was that self-reliance of yours when you left me alone in the slaughter of Ahi?
For I am indeed fierce, powerful, and mighty; with my weapons, I have bowed down every enemy.
O Bull, you have performed many deeds for us with our allied and equal manly powers.
For we shall indeed accomplish many things, O most mighty Indra, through our resolve, whatever we may desire, O Maruts.
O Maruts, with my own Indra-power I slew Vṛtra;
having become mighty through my own fury, I, the thunderbolt-armed one, have made these all-glittering waters easy to pass for Manu.
Nothing is superior to you, O Maghavan; indeed, no one among the gods is known to be your equal.
Neither one being born nor one already born can attain it. Do what you must do, O you who have grown great!

Though I am alone, let my power be manifold; whatever I, being bold, shall accomplish through my wisdom—O Maruts, I am indeed known as the fierce one; Indra alone is the lord of those things which I have set in motion.
