O Maruts, you have gladdened me here with this hymn, since you, O heroes, have fashioned for me a sacred prayer worthy of renown—
for Indra, the bull, the great warrior— for me, as friends for a friend, with your own bodies for my body.
Truly, these Maruts, shining toward me, free from blemish and bestowing glory— having been beheld, they, who are of moon-like hue, have pleased me and continue to please me even now.
Who here among you, O Maruts, has magnified you? Come forward, O friends, toward your friends! Stirring up their wondrous thoughts, become aware of these my sacred truths.
Since the inspired wisdom of Mānya has brought us here to serve you, as a poet serves for his own service—O Maruts, turn hither quickly to the sage; the singer has recited these prayers for you.
This is your hymn, O Maruts, this is the song of Māndārya, the son of Māna, the poet. May it bring offspring for our own bodies; may we find strengthening food that bestows long life.
Let us now proclaim that former greatness of the impetuous host, the herald of the Bull.
Like kindling wood on your march, O Maruts, you who roar aloud; like warriors in battle, O Śakras, display your powers.
Constantly bringing sweetness like a son, they play at play in the sacrificial assemblies, impetuous in their vigor.
The Rudras reach out with protection to the one who bows; possessing their own inherent strength, they do not neglect the one who offers oblations.
To him who has offered oblations, the immortal helpers have granted abundance of wealth;
for him the Maruts, like well-disposed friends, sprinkle many regions with refreshing milk.
Those who have clothed themselves in the regions with their powers, your swift-moving steeds have rushed forward.
All beings, even the dwellings of men, are afraid; wondrous is your march when your spears are extended.

When they, the manly ones, with flashing luster, made the mountains roar or shook the very back of heaven, every lord of the forest fears you at your onset; the plants fly apart like those seeking to escape a chariot.
O fierce Maruts, with your benevolence, you whose hosts are unharmed, fulfill our desire;
where your lightning, with its gnashing teeth, bites, it releases the cattle like a well-aimed weapon with its force.

They who grant firm support, whose bounty is inexhaustible, who do not withhold their gifts, and who are well-praised in the assemblies—these ones sing their song for the drinking of the intoxicating juice; they know the first heroic deeds of the hero.

O Maruts, protect with your hundredfold arms that man from treachery and evil whom you have favored; O fierce, powerful, and exuberant ones, guard that person from reproach for the sake of the prosperity of his offspring.
O Maruts, all auspicious things are placed upon your chariots; as if in rivalry with one another, your powers are set there.
Rings are upon your shoulders for the long journeys; your axle revolves right between the two wheels.
Many auspicious things are upon their manly arms; upon their chests are golden ornaments, impetuous and glittering.
Upon their shoulders are these [spears], and upon their fellies are sharp blades; like birds spreading their wings, they have displayed their splendors.
Great by their greatness, far-reaching in their power, visible from afar like the heavens with their stars;
sweet-toned, fair-tongued, sounding with their mouths, the Maruts, mingling with Indra, chant their hymns around him.
O well-born Maruts, that is your greatness; long-lasting is your bounty, like the ordinance of Aditi.
Even Indra cannot, by his abandonment, frustrate that [bounty] which you have bestowed upon the man of good deeds.

O Maruts, that kinship of yours which you, the immortals, maintained in a former age—manifesting many blessings—through this prayer you have granted hearing to Manu; together with wondrous deeds, O heroes, you have made yourselves known.
O Maruts, swift ones, by means of your abundant wealth may we flourish for a long time;
when men extend their efforts in the assembly, may I attain that desired goal through these sacrifices.
This hymn for you, O Maruts, this song of the poet Māndārya, son of Māna—may it bring offspring for our own bodies; may we find strengthening food and a community that bestows life-sustaining gifts.
A thousand are your aids for us, O Indra; a thousand are the most praiseworthy refreshments, O Lord of the Bay Steeds.
A thousand riches are for our delight; may thousandfold strengths come unto us.

May the Maruts come toward us with their aids— those of highest rank or those dwelling in the great heaven, they who possess wondrous power— especially when their teams of horses, even from the farthest distance, hasten on the very further shore of the ocean.
Among them the well-placed, butter-smeared [ladle] has clung, like a spear with golden sheath held close at hand;
moving in secret like a woman among men, the speech gathers together like an assembly in a hall.
The bright, tireless Maruts have mingled with the youthful [waters] as if they were common property.
The terrible gods did not push away heaven and earth; they accepted the strengthening [offering] for friendship.
When the divine Rodasī, with loosened locks and manly spirit,
was pleased to accompany him, she— like Sūryā, with her brilliant countenance— ascended the chariot of her worshipper like the onset of a cloud.
The youths established the young woman, who is united with splendor and firm in the assemblies;
when your hymn, O Maruts, accompanied by oblations, and the one who has pressed the Soma, sings the song in worship.
I proclaim that which is worthy of being proclaimed— the true greatness of these Maruts— when they,
of virile mind and defiant spirit, carry along with them even firm and fortunate women.
Mitra and Varuṇa protect [us] from blame; Aryaman removes those who are unworthy of praise.
Even the unshakable and firm things are moved; the Maruts, who grant precious boons, have caused them to grow.
O Maruts, there is indeed no end to your power, even from afar; it has reached us.
Having increased with bold strength, they have boldly cast off their enmity like a wave.
May we today be the dearest to Indra, and may we call upon him tomorrow in the assembly;
may we be so in the past, and may he follow us through our great days—may Ṛbhukṣan favor us, O heroes.
This hymn is for you, O Maruts; this song is from the poet Māndārya, the son of Māna.
May this [prayer] bring offspring for our own bodies; may we find strengthening food that bestows long life.
Sacrifice after sacrifice, you who are swift in action, come together; with every prayer, you, O gods, accept our devotion.
For the sake of well-being for both worlds, may I turn you hither with beautiful hymns for great protection.
Like self-born bulls, those who are self-strong, the shakers have been born for food and for heaven;
they are like the thousandfold surges of the waters, like cows to be praised with the mouth, like stallions.
Like Soma juices pressed out, with their stalks satisfied, they sit within the hearts as if drunk; like those who offer service, they dwell there.
Upon their shoulders, as if clinging vines, something clings fast; in their hands, both the ring and the knife are joined together.
Yoked by themselves, the immortals have come down from heaven at their will; urge yourselves on with the whip!
Born of many powers, the Maruts, whose spears are flashing, have shaken even the firmest things, being free from dust.
O Maruts, who among you—armed with spears and flashing like lightning—trembles by his own power, as if with a tongue between his jaws?
Like the discharge of arrows on the path of a journey, they move across the desert, many-impelled, like the sun’s steed Etaśa day by day.

Where indeed is the farthest limit of this great space, and where its nearest end, O Maruts, in which you have come? When you cause that which is joined together to fall apart as if it were fragile, you fly with the stone through the shimmering ocean.
Like a victorious prize for you, O Maruts, is that overwhelming, sun-bright, brilliant, and crushing force;
auspicious is your bounty, like the sacrificial fee of one who gives, wide-spreading and flashing like the power of the Asuras.
The rivers roar against the tires [of their chariots] when they send forth their thunderous voice from the clouds;
the lightnings smile down upon the earth when the Maruts sprinkle the ghee.
Pṛśni brought forth for the great battle the brilliant host of the tireless Maruts;
those companions gave birth to the formidable being, and then they beheld their own vigorous power.

This hymn for you, O Maruts, this song of the poet Māndārya, the son of Māna—may it bring offspring for our own bodies; may we find strengthening food and a community that bestows life-sustaining gifts.

O Indra, you are indeed great since you [protect] these; you are the protector against even great hostility. As such, O wise ordainer, grant us the favor of the Maruts, for those [favors] are most dear to you.
O Indra, those Maruts have yoked their teams, being conscious of their invincibility among mortals; the host of Maruts, eager for combat, hastens to win the prize in the struggle for the light.

O Indra, that spear of yours has been fixed for us; the Maruts drive forth their formidable power in its entirety. For even Agni, blazing brightly in the wind, bestows nourishments like waters upon an island.
O Indra, do you indeed grant us that wealth, as a gift with most powerful sacrificial fees;
may those hymns of praise which have pleased you, O Vāyu, cause you to swell with strength like the breast of honey.
In you, O Indra, are the most bountiful riches that lead every one who follows the *ṛta*.
May those Maruts be gracious to us—those gods who of old were like those seeking a path.
Go forth toward the liberal men, O Indra; exert yourself in the great earthly dwelling.
For when their broad-based [chariots] have stood there, like women at a ford, they display their manly deeds.
One hears the approaching roar of these terrible, tireless Maruts as they advance;
they who, with their aids, strike down the mortal who attacks them in battle, like debtors, with their rushing charges.
O Indra, together with the Maruts, bestow upon us for all people treasures headed by cattle;
O God, being praised by the gods, you are praised in turn. May we find strengthening food that grants life-sustaining gifts.
There is nothing now, nor will there be tomorrow; who knows that which is mysterious?
One must proceed with caution regarding the mind of another, for even what has been learned may perish.
O Indra, why do you wish to strike us? The Maruts are your brothers;
act rightly with them, and do not slay us in the encounter.
O brother Agastya, why do you disregard us, being our friend? For we know how your mind is; you simply do not wish to give to us.
Let them prepare the altar; let them kindle the fire in front.
There, we two shall extend for you the sacrifice, the manifestation of immortality.
O Lord of wealth, you rule over riches; O Lord of friends, you are the most liberal among friends.
O Indra, consult with the Maruts, and then consume the oblations in due season.
With this homage and with this hymn, I approach you; I beg for the goodwill of the swift ones. O Maruts, bestowing [gifts] through your wisdom, lay aside your anger and unyoke your horses.

O Maruts, this hymn of yours, fashioned with the heart and mind, has been offered to you with reverence, O gods. Come hither, taking pleasure in it with your minds, for you are indeed the increasers of our homage.

May our Maruts, being praised, show us mercy; and may Maghavan, the most beneficent, being praised, do the same. May our cherished forests stand upright; O Maruts, may we conquer all the days in our desire for victory.
Fleeing from this powerful Indra in fear, O Maruts, I was trembling;
for you, the oblations were prepared and sharpened, but we have set them aside—be gracious unto us.

By whom even the Mānasas were made conscious at the dawning of the eternal mornings through his might—may he, the bull, together with the Maruts, bestow glory upon us; he who is fierce with the fierce, ancient, and the giver of victory.
O Indra, protect the men who are more powerful; together with the Maruts, be one whose wrath is averted.
Endowed with excellent wisdom and victorious, may we find a strengthening realm that bestows life-giving gifts.
May your journey be wondrous, and wondrous your aid, O bounteous Maruts, who shine with the splendor of serpents.
Far away from us, O bounteous Maruts, let that rushing arrow of yours be; far away the stone which you hurl.
O bounteous ones, spare the people of Tṛṇaskanda;
raise us up that we may live.

Sing the *sāman* like the bird of the atmosphere; let us praise that which has grown strong and is full of light. The milch-cows, the inviolable ones, are upon the sacred grass (*barhis*), as they seek to win the divine dwelling.
The bull shall sing with the bulls who offer sweat as oblation; like a ravenous wild beast, he shall leap beyond the one who would revile him.
The exhilarating Hotṛ, praised by men, brings forth the two pairs of thoughts; the worshipful youth bears them forward.
May the Hotṛ-priest reach the measured seats as he goes; may he bear the germ of the earth through the autumns.
Let the horse neigh as he is led, let the bull bellow; let the voice move between the two worlds like a messenger.
To him, those who seek the gods bring forth deeds and mighty exploits;
may Indra, of wondrous luster, take pleasure in them, standing upon his chariot as one easily accessible, like the two Nāsatyas.
Praise that Indra indeed, who is a warrior, who is the hero, the bountiful lord, who stands upon the chariot;
who, possessed of strength, is a better fighter even than those facing him, and who is the dispeller of even the dense darkness.

Since he thus prevails in greatness over men, the two worlds, heaven and earth, are not sufficient for his girth; Indra has encompassed them as if they were a fold of land. Self-sustaining, he bears up the sky like a crest-ornament.
In battles, O hero, we would fain honor you, the protector of the virtuous and the foremost traveler;
for in the exhilaration of the draught, the united hosts—those who rejoice with the patron in spoils—exalt Indra.
For thus indeed are the libations a joy for you in the ocean, when the divine waters rejoice in them;
every cow has become pleasing to you, even when you, through your inspired thought, visit the people of the patrons.
May we be his good friends through these praises, like those of men who possess excellent protection;
may Indra abide in our hymns of praise, as one swift in action brings forth our songs of laudation.
Like men vying with one another in their praises, may Indra, the wielder of the thunderbolt, be on our side;
like those seeking a friend, they serve the Lord of the City with well-guided sacrifices, seeking him as the center.
For indeed, any sacrifice that offends Indra, even if it proceeds crookedly with a wandering mind,
brings him home— just as one reaches a watering-place when thirsty, or as a long journey brings the successful traveler to his goal.
O Indra, do not fail us here in battles along with the gods, for you, O mighty one, possess the power to overcome.
Even the great host of the bounteous Maruts, whose youthful power is joined with the oblation, is praised by the song of him who offers the sacrifice.

This hymn of praise, O Indra, is for you; by this, O Lord of Bay Steeds, find a path for us. O God, turn us toward prosperity. May we find a strengthening community that bestows life-sustaining gifts.
O Indra, king of kings, and you gods, protect us; O Asura, guard us!
You are the lord of the virtuous, our bounteous deliverer; you are the true one, the possessor of wealth, the giver of strength.
O Indra, you shattered the seven autumnal fortresses that were the refuge of the Dānu people who spoke with insults;
O blameless one, you released the waters of the flood and delivered Vṛtra over to the young Purukutsa.
O Indra, much-invoked one, with those [helpers] by whom you now encompassed the unassailable ones who have heroes for their lords,
and the heavens— [with them] you, like a lion in its den, performed deeds for the sake of the one who dwells in the waters, the insatiable Agni Tūrvayāṇa.
O Indra, may they remain for you in this same place for the praise of your greatness through the thunderbolt;
when you released the floods and the cattle by battle, you stood with your two bay horses and boldly seized the spoils of war.
O Indra, carry Kutsa, in whom you take delight; let the two bay steeds of Vāta, Syūmanyu and Ṛjra, draw you.
Let the Sun’s wheel be cast forward in the encounter; may he whose arm wields the thunderbolt go forth against his rivals.
O Indra, lord of bay horses, strengthened by the libations, you have struck down the non-givers who were like Mīḍhus,
they who looked upon Aryaman together with their kin, but were shattered by you while carrying away their offspring.
The seer, whispering in the contest for the sun, made the earth a pillow for the Dāsa. Maghavan performed three wondrous deeds; he cast Kuyavāc into a pitless place within his dwelling.
Those ancient deeds of yours, O Indra, have come forth anew; you brought down many clouds for the sake of light.
You shattered the godless fortresses as if they were unbaked clay; you struck down the weapon of the godless oppressor.
O Indra, you, the shaker, sent forth the shaking waters like flowing rivers;
when, O hero, you carried across the ocean, you brought Turvaśa and Yadu safely to the further shore.

O Indra, may you be ours at all times, the most effective protector of men against the wolf. As such, grant us victory over all our rivals; may we find a strengthening community that bestows life-sustaining gifts.
O Lord of the Bay Steeds, your exhilarating, intoxicating drink has been drunk for your greatness, as if from a large vessel.
O Bull, your bull-like *indu* is a prize-winning steed that wins a thousandfold.
May your exhilarating, bull-like, and most excellent intoxication come to us— O Indra, the immortal one, the victorious, the winner of spoils, the subduer of hostile armies.
For you, O hero, are the winner; you urge on the chariot of man. As one who is victorious, burn up the lawless Dasyu with your flame, as if a vessel with fire.
O Sage, as the sovereign lord, you stole the wheel of the sun by your might;
carry Kutsa, the weapon for Śuṣṇa, with the horses of Vāta.
For most intoxicating is your exhilaration, and most splendid is your power;
as a slayer of Vṛtra and a finder of wide space, may you consider yourself the best winner of horses.
Just as you were for the ancient singers, O Indra, like water for one who thirsts, so do I cry out to you with this invocation. May we find this strengthening food that bestows long life.
Make us exhilarated for the seeking of wealth; O Indu, as a bull, enter Indra.
Raging in your fury, you drive away the enemy; you find no one standing before you.
Direct our songs toward him who alone moves among the people;
he toward whom the self-power (svadhā) is sown, as a bull plows the barley.
In whose two hands are all the treasures of the five peoples;
be on the watch for him who seeks to harm us and strike him down like a thunderbolt from heaven.
Slay the one who does not press the soma, the difficult-to-reach one who brings you no joy;
bestow upon us his possession, for even a patron desires it.
O Indu, you have helped that Indra of double strength in his hymns, being ever-present; you have helped the vigorous one in the race for booty during the contests.
As you were to the ancient singers, O Indra, like water for one who thirsts, so do I call upon you with this invocation. May we find strengthening food that bestows long life.
The bull among men, the king of the peoples, Indra, invoked by many, who fills the dwellings—
being praised and seeking glory, come hither to me with your aid, having yoked your two vigorous bay steeds.
O Indra, those bulls of yours, the stallions yoked by prayer, the coursers with powerful chariots—mount them! Come hither with them; we invoke you, O Indra, when the Soma is pressed.
Mount the bull-chariot; O Bull, the Soma is pressed for you and the sweet juices are poured out.
Having yoked the two bay steeds, O Bull of the peoples, come toward me down the steep slope.

This sacrifice goes to the gods; this is the sacrificial food; these are the sacred prayers; this, O Indra, is the Soma. The sacred grass is strewn; come hither, O Śakra, sit down and drink; unyoke your two bay horses here.
O Indra, well-praised, come hither toward the sacred formulations (*brahmāṇi*) of the poet Mānya.
Singing your praises, may we find the light of day through your protection; may we find strengthening food that bestows long life.

O Indra, whatever readiness of ear you have, by which you have become a helper for those who sing your praises—do not consume our desire as it grows; may I obtain all [the fruits] of your work from the living man.
O Indra, King of kings, let them not deceive us, whatever two sisters may do in the womb;
even the waters have sped toward him with swift motion—may Indra come to our friendship and vigor.
Indra, the hero, is the victor with men in battles; he is the hearer of the call of the singer who implores him.
He brings his chariot near to the donor; he raises up our songs when he is present in person.
Thus, through the men, Indra has become renowned for his glorious fame; he, the devourer of nourishment, has come to the side of those who possess friends.
In the assembly and in the contest for food, the praise of the sacrificer is celebrated as the all-effecting deed.
With you, O Maghavan Indra, may we overcome our enemies who deem themselves great.
You are our protector; you indeed have been for our prosperity. May we find this strengthening food that bestows long life.
"Many autumns have I spent in toil, through nights and mornings as the dawns wear me out.
Old age diminishes the beauty of our bodies; yet even now, let husbands come to their wives."

For even those who were the first observers of the *ṛta*, who spoke the truths together with the gods—they too have passed away, for they did not reach the end. Now let the wives come together with the bulls.
The toil is not in vain, since the gods protect us; may we overcome all rivalries.
Here let us proclaim the victory in the hundred-pathed contest, as we two, a harmonious pair, have come together.
Desire has come upon me from this side or from that, from somewhere or other, as if from a withholding river.
Lopāmudrā leads forth the bull; the unwise woman suckles the wise one who is panting.
I now address this Soma, drunk within my heart from close at hand:
whatever offense we have committed against it, may he forgive that, for mortal man has many desires.
Agastya, digging with his spades and desiring offspring, progeny, and strength—
the fierce seer nourished both castes and attained true blessings among the gods.
Your well-governed horses traverse the realms when your chariot flies around the watery expanses.
Your golden fellies scatter spray; drinking of the sweetness, you accompany the dawns.
You two reach down to the steed when he, the manly one who strives in sacrifice, is falling away;
when your sister, praised by all, brings [the oblation] for you both, she seeks food and the drinking of the honeyed draught for the sake of strength.
You two placed the milk within the raw cow, the primordial essence of the cow;
when the pure, oblation-bearing one, like a cleansing ladle, offers the sacrifice between the two fire-sticks that consume the wood.
For Atri, you two chose the honeyed *gharma* for his seeking, like a flood of water;
O Aśvins, heroes, that [work] of yours regarding the desire for cattle proceeds toward the sweetness like the wheels of a chariot.
O Wonder-workers, may I turn you both hither for the sake of giving, as the aged Tugrya did with his longing for cattle;
your greatness accompanies the waters and the two worlds; O Holy Ones, your swift eye has turned away from distress.
When you two, O bounteous ones, yoke your teams of horses, you release Purandhi by your own powers;
like the wind, the patron hastens and exerts himself; like one of holy vows, he wins the prize for the great purpose.
For we indeed, as your praisers, truly celebrate you both; even the niggardly Paṇi, though intent on his own gain, has been surpassed.
And so, O blameless Aśvins, you two bulls indeed protect the god who stands near.
For you two, O Aśvins, indeed day after day, even at the winning of the flowing stream of Virudra,
Agastya— most praised among men among men— made himself known by thousands, like one who strikes with a weapon.

When you two advance with the greatness of your chariot, you go forth swiftly like the *hotṛ* of a man. Bestow upon our patrons, O Nāsatyas, wealth consisting of fine horses; may we be possessors of riches.

O Aśvins, we invoke today that chariot of yours with new hymns for our well-being—the chariot with uninjured fellies, which traverses the sky. May we find a food-providing community that grants life-sustaining gifts.
When, O most beloved ones, do you, acting as *adhvaryu*s, draw forth the waters with food and riches? This sacrifice has offered praise to you both, O dispensers of wealth, protectors of men.
May your pure, water-drinking horses— divine coursers with the speed of the wind,
swift as thought, vigorous, and smooth-backed— bring you hither, O self-ruling Aśvins.
May your chariot, like a rushing torrent, come with its wide seat for our prosperity—
swift as thought, the first to arrive, worthy of sacrifice, and full of power, O you who are mindful of the worshiper.
Born here and there, they have lowed together with their stainless bodies and their own names.
One of you is the victorious patron of the fair sacrifice; the other is the fortunate son of heaven.
May your tawny, towering steed, moving downward according to our will, come to our dwellings.
May the two bay horses of the other [Aśvin] swell with strength; O Aśvins, may they stir the regions with their neighing.
Like a bull, the autumnal showerer comes forth for you both; he moves about, bestowing many refreshments of honeyed sweetness.
By the ways of the other, they have been nourished with strengths; like surging rivers, the waters have come to us.
An ancient song has been released for you two by the wise poet, O Aśvins, flowing in three ways even in its strength.
You who are praised, protect the one who implores you; on your journey, hear my call, even though you are not traveling.
Moreover, this song of yours, belonging to the bright and radiant one, swells in the assembly where the threefold sacred grass is spread for the sake of men.
O showerers, your bull-like cloud has overflowed, bestowing gifts upon man like the pouring out of milk from a cow.
O Aśvins, like Pūṣan, the one rich in wisdom honors you both as one honors Agni or Uṣas with oblations;
when I, praising you for the sake of wide space, call upon you, may we find a strengthening community that bestows swift gifts.
This wisdom has come into being; now let it be honored! O wise ones, rejoice in the chariot that bears the bull.
You who quicken the prayer, you who are worthy of worship, you who possess the wealth of Viśpalā, you two sons of heaven, pure in your vows for the sake of the righteous doer.
For you two are most like Indra, worthy of praise, most like Maruts, most wondrous in your deeds, the best of charioteers among those who drive the chariot.
You carry a full chariot laden with sweetness; with that, O Aśvins, come to the donor.
O Wonder-workers, what do you do here? What do you sit for, [regarding] that person who, though offering no oblation, exalts himself?
Pass him by; let the life of the stingy one decay. Create light for the inspired singer who utters his hymns.
Crush the dogs that bark on every side; slay the adversaries, O Aśvins, for you understand these things.
Make every word of the singer rich in treasure; O Nāsatyas, both of you, protect my praise.
You two fashioned this winged boat, endowed with life, for the son of Tugra upon the rivers;
with which you, with godward intent, carried him forth, and flew with easy flight from the great flood.
The son of Tugra was cast down into the waters, abandoned in darkness where there is no support;
four ships, beloved by Jaṭhara, sent forth by the Aśvins, carry him across.
What tree was that which stood firm in the midst of the ocean, which the son of Tugra, when in distress, embraced?
Like the feathers of a swift-flying bird, O Aśvins, you took hold of it and carried him away for the sake of glory.
O Nāsatyas, O Heroes, may that hymn which the Mānas have uttered for you follow after you.
From this Soma-offering assembly today, may we find a strengthening community that bestows life-sustaining gifts.
Yoke that [chariot] which is swifter than thought, O Mighty Ones, which has three seats and three wheels;
with it you approach the dwelling of the pious man, and with its triple-layered [structure] you fly like birds on their wings.

The well-rolling chariot moves as it approaches the earth, when you two, possessed of wisdom, stand ready for the strengthening food. May this beautiful song attend your wondrous form; O Daughters of Heaven, you two accompany the Dawn.
Mount your well-rolling chariot, which follows your sacred laws, O possessors of oblations—
by means of which, O Nāsatyas, O Heroes, you come to our dwelling to provide for us, for our offspring, and for ourselves.
Let not the wolf nor the she-wolf harm you; do not avoid us, nor cast us aside. This portion is set out for you, this song; O wonder-workers, these are your vessels of honeyed draughts.
Gotama, Purumīḷha, and Atri, bearing oblations, invoke you both, O wonder-workers, for protection.
Like one who points out the direction, like two who travel straight toward a goal, O Nāsatyas, come to my invocation.
We have crossed to the further shore of this darkness; our hymn of praise has been offered to you both, O Aśvins.
Come hither by the paths traveled by the gods; may we find strengthening food that bestows long life.
We invoke you two today, and we shall invoke you again when the dawn breaks with our hymns—
the two Nāsatyas, wherever they may be, the sons of Heaven, most liberal givers for the sake of the pious man.
O Bull-like ones, rejoice well among us; slay the Paṇis, exulting in the flowing stream. Hear me through the invocations of my hymns, O Heroes, you who are seekers and perceivers with your ears.

For glory, O Pūṣan, like two arrow-makers, the divine Nāsatyas prepared the bridal procession for Sūryā. Your towering steeds, born of the waters, move forward like the worn-out ages of the mighty Varuṇa.
O lovers of sweetness, may that gift of yours be with us; further the hymn of the poet Mānya.
When, O bounteous givers, men rejoice in your glorious deeds for the sake of heroic power.
This hymn has been fashioned for you both, O Aśvins, with well-wrought praise by the Mānas, O bounteous lords.
Come on your path for our offspring and for ourselves, rejoicing in the house of Agastya, O Nāsatyas.
We have crossed to the further shore of this darkness; our hymn of praise has been offered to you both, O Aśvins.
Come hither by the paths traveled by the gods; may we find strengthening food that bestows long life.
Which of these two is the earlier, which the later? O sages, how were they born? Who truly knows?
They both support the universe by their own power; as for their name, the two days revolve like two wheels.
The two footless ones bear as their offspring the many-footed embryo that moves;
like a son ever in the lap of his parents, O Heaven and Earth, protect us from evil.
I invoke the unassailable gift of Aditi, which is blameless, heavenly, free from harm, and accompanied by homage.
O Heaven and Earth, produce that for the singer; O Heaven and Earth, protect us from evil.
May we follow the two world-halves, Rodasī, who are free from heat and provide protection, whose sons are the gods;
O both worlds, protect us from evil with the help of both gods throughout the days.
When the two young maidens, sisters and kinswomen, come together with their borders meeting in the lap of their parents;
when they kiss the navel of the world—O Heaven and Earth, protect us from evil!

I invoke with the aid of the gods the two wide, great, and lofty seats, the parents of all beings, who by the Eternal Law (ṛta) bestow immortality and possess beautiful countenances. O Heaven and Earth, protect us from evil!
The two wide, broad, vast, and far-extending ones I address with reverence at this sacrifice—those two auspicious ones who bestow great success; O Heaven and Earth, protect us from evil.
Whatever sin we have committed against the gods, or against a friend, or even against the lord of the house—may this prayer be an atonement for them;
O Heaven and Earth, protect us from evil!
May both noble praises protect me; may both assist me with aid and favor.
O gods, even against the great enemy, may we, rejoicing, find strength for the sake of the most bountiful giver.

I, the wise one, have proclaimed this Truth (*ṛta*) to Heaven and Earth so that it may be heard far and wide for the first time. May Father and Mother protect me from reproach and from misfortune in the encounter; may they guard me with their aids.

O Heaven and Earth, O Father and Mother, may this which I address to you here be true. Be present with your protections, O lowest of the gods; may we find a strengthening community that grants life-sustaining gifts.

May Savitṛ, the god who belongs to all men, come to our sacrifice with nourishing offerings and fair praise; so that you young ones may exhilarate us, and that the whole world may be mindful [of us] at the time of rest.
May all the gods come to us, united— Mitra, Aryaman, and Varuṇa— together,
so that they may all be our strengtheners and make our power invincible, like a firm fortress.
I praise with hymns Agni, your most beloved guest, who is victorious and well-disposed;
so that Varuṇa may be our glory, and the unassailable patron may bring us strengthening food.

I approach you both with homage, O Dawn and Night, who strive for victory, like a cow easy to milk; on the same day, I measure out my hymn between you two, who possess different forms yet share the same udder of milk.

And may Ahi Budhnya grant us joy; like a cow swelling with milk for her calf, the Sindhu river yearns for him, by whom we urge on the grandson of the waters—he whom the stallions, swift as thought, carry along.
And may Tvaṣṭṛ come toward us, in harmony with the patrons at the time of the pressing;
may Indra, the slayer of Vṛtra, the protector of the people, the most powerful among men, come here to us.
And our hymns, yoked with horses, lick him as cows lick their young calf;
our songs embrace him, the most fragrant of men, as wives embrace their husbands.
And may the Maruts with their increased armies sit down with us, together with Rodasī, being of one mind;
they whose horses are spotted like rushing streams, who destroy the enemies, and who are gods bound by friendship.
When they have manifested themselves through their greatness, they yoke their well-prepared teams with a perfect hymn. Then, like a bolt on a fair day, their armies drench the entire enemy host.
Bring the Aśvins forward for our protection; bring Pūṣan forward, for they are self-strong. Viṣṇu is free from malice, as are Vāta and Ṛbhukṣan; may I turn the gods hitherward for their favor.

O worshipful ones, may this our devotion toward you be full and provide us with a dwelling; may it strive among the gods for wealth. May we find a strengthening community that grants life-sustaining gifts.
Now I shall praise Food, the great upholder of laws and power,
by whose might Trita shattered Vṛtra limb from limb.
O sweet Soma, O honeyed Soma, we have chosen you;
be our protector.
Come to us, O Soma, as a father, auspicious with your auspicious aids; bringing delight, not to be hated, a friend most kind and free from duplicity.
O Food, those juices of yours are spread across the realms,
resting in heaven like the winds.
O *pitu*, these [streams] of yours bestow gifts; O most sweet *pitu* of yours, the flavors of your juices, being full of vigor, rush forth like those with thick necks.
In thee, O Food, the mind of the great gods is fixed;
by thy beautiful banner it has been made manifest, and with thy help thou hast slain the dragon.
O Soma, when you have gone there, O food, to the radiant heights of the mountains, even from there, O sweet food, come to us to be our portion.
Whatever essence of the waters and plants we consume,
O Vātāpi, become fatness for us.
O Soma, whatever portion of ours you enjoy that is mixed with milk, mixed with curds, or mixed with barley— O Vātāpi, become fat indeed.
O herb, become a gruel; be fat, a kidney, and a source of nourishment. O drinker of the wind, become indeed fat.
O Soma, Father, we have refined you with our words, as cows prepare their offerings;
you who provide a feast together with the gods, we make you a feast-companion for us.
Kindled today, you shine as a god among the gods, O conqueror of thousands;
as the messenger and sage, carry the oblations.
Tanūnapāt, for the one who goes toward the *ṛta*, the sacrifice is anointed with honey;
may he bestow thousandfold nourishments.
Being invoked and worthy of praise, bring here the gods who are worthy of sacrifice;
O Agni, you are the winner of thousands.
With power they have strewn the eastward-pointing sacrificial grass, yielding a thousand heroes,
where you, O Ādityas, shine forth in splendor.
The Virāj, the Samrāj, the Vibhvīs, and the Prabhvīs— those which are many and even more numerous—
the doors have flowed with clarified butter.
For the two Dawns, adorned with beautiful gold and fine ornaments, shine forth with splendor; may they both sit here in this place.
For the two divine Hotṛ-priests, the sages of eloquent speech, shall indeed perform this sacrifice of ours as the first.
O Bhāratī, Iḷā, Sarasvatī— O all of you whom I invoke,
impel us toward prosperity.
For Tvaṣṭṛ, the lord, has fashioned all forms and all cattle; worship so that their abundance may come to us.
O Lord of the Forest, by your own power release the path for the gods;
may Agni make the oblations sweet.
Agni, the leader of the gods, is anointed with the Gāyatra hymn;
he shines forth amidst the utterances of Svāhā.
O Agni, lead us by a good path to wealth, O God who knowest all ways;
keep far from us the sin that leads astray, and we shall offer unto thee the most abundant speech of homage.

O Agni, as one who is ever new, carry us across all difficulties with blessings. May you be a broad, vast, and wide fortress for us; be a source of well-being and joy for our children and descendants.
O Agni, keep disease away from us; let those who do not protect with fire fall upon the people.
O God, worthy of sacrifice, together with all the immortals, grant us the earth again for our well-being.
Protect us, O Agni, with your unfailing protections, shining brightly in your beloved dwelling.
O youngest one, may no danger reach your singer now or in the future, O powerful lord.
O Agni, do not deliver us over to the malevolent, the greedy enemy, or to misfortune.
Do not surrender us to one who bites, nor to one who strikes, nor to one who seeks to harm us; O Lord of Might, protect us!

O Agni, born of Truth, may one like you, being praised, grant protection to our person. You are indeed the one who drives away all those who wish to harm or revile us; for you, O God, are the discerning dispeller.
O Agni, you who know both of them, you approach at the onset of day for the sake of man, O worshipful one;
at the arrival of evening, you become one to be commanded by man, like a stallion to be groomed by the eager ones.
We have uttered our invocations to this victorious Agni, the son of Manu.
May we, together with a thousand seers, win a thousandfold; may we find strengthening food that bestows long life.
Exalt with new hymns Bṛhaspati, the unassailable bull whose tongue is sweet;
he who is the leader of songs, radiant, and whose praises the gods and mortals alike listen to when he utters them.
To him, the timely words of praise resort, he who has been released like the outpouring of those seeking the gods;
for Bṛhaspati, moving straight toward his desires, has become all-pervasive through the cosmic order, even as Mātariśvan.
He extends his arms like Savitṛ toward the hymn of praise, the offering of homage, and the song of glory;
by his wisdom, he is one who strikes on the day, terrible like a wild beast, yet free from malice and full of power.

His fame resounds in heaven and upon earth; like a swift steed, he, the wise possessor of sacrificial wealth, restrains [the foe]. Like the weapons of wild beasts, these [powers] of Bṛhaspati, possessing serpent-like magic, advance toward the heavens.
Those wicked Pajras who, regarding you as a mere god of the sacrificial residue, live off your blessings—O Bṛhaspati, you do not bestow wealth upon the evil-minded; rather, you consume the scorner.
Like a well-trodden path leading to good pastures, like a beloved friend who is difficult to resist;
those who are unassailable and look upon us have stood there, uncovering what was veiled.
To him whom the hymns go together like rivers, like streams with banks and wheels toward the ocean—to that wise Bṛhaspati, the vulture, looks upon both from within: the waters and the crossing.

Thus has the great, many-born, and powerful god Bṛhaspati been established as a bull. May he, when praised by us, bestow wealth in heroes and cattle; may we find a strengthening community that grants life-sustaining gifts.
Like the *kaṅkata* bird, not like the *kaṅkata*, and like the *satīnakaṅkata*—
these two, called "the swarms," unseen, have smeared themselves.
She strikes those who have not yet been seen as she approaches, and she strikes them as she departs;
moreover, she strikes while pounding, and she grinds while grinding.
The *śarāsa*, *kuśarāsa*, *darbha*, and *sairyā* grasses, as well as the *mauñja*,
*adṛṣṭa*, and *vairiṇa*— all these together have been smeared [with poison].
The cows have settled in the stall; the wild beasts have entered their lairs;
the lights of men have gone out; and the unseen ones have smeared themselves.
These very ones have appeared at nightfall like thieves;
though unseen before, you have now become seen by all—you have been discovered.
Heaven is your father, Earth your mother, Soma your brother, and Aditi your sister;
unseen yet seen by all, stay here and rest in comfort.
Those that are on the shoulders, those that are on the limbs, those that are needle-like, and those that are prickly— whatever invisible things you are here, all of you together, perish!
The Sun rises in the east, seen by all, the slayer of the unseen;
crushing all unseen beings and all female sorceresses.
Yonder sun has flown up, consuming all things manifold;
the Āditya, visible from every mountain, is the destroyer of the unseen.
I hang the poison in the sun; I place the skin-bag in the house of the one who possesses the spirituous liquor.
May it surely not kill us, nor may we die; its range is far, yet the one who stands upon the bay horses has made you sweet with honey.
This tiny little bird has swallowed your poison;
it shall surely not die, nor shall we die. The one who stands upon the bay horses has made its range a league; honey has made you sweet.
The thrice-seven sparks have consumed the flower of the poison.
They indeed do not die, nor shall we die; the one who stands upon the bay horses has made your range free from death, and honeyed sweetness has made you sweet.
Of the ninety-nine new [stems] that cause the growth of poison, I have grasped the names of them all. O enemy, its range is a yojana; it stands upon the sun, and the honeyed one has made you sweet.
The thrice-seven peahens, the seven sisters, the maidens—
may they carry away your poison like women carrying water in jars.
So small is the *kuṣumbhaka* worm; with a stone I crush it.
From there the poison has turned away, following the distant enclosures.
The Kuṣumbhaka, as he was rolling down from the mountain, said this:
"The venom of the scorpion is sapless; O scorpion, your venom is sapless."
